utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14-PT, the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: May I have appearances for the parties, please? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Good morning, your Honour, I am the Prosecutor, and my name is Louise Arbour. Appearing with me is Professor Peter Crawford and Mr Mark Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. My name is Russell Hayman. I am appearing on behalf of General Tihomir Blaskic. I appear also with my co-counsel Anto Nobilo. I went looking for General Blaskic this morning. I do not see him here. He has not waived his appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I was not aware of, Mr Hayman, that General Blaskic -- that you wished to have General Blaskic here. You are not actually a party to these proceedings. We did invite you to be present, since you have also requested that a subpoena be issued. So we are inviting you really, not as a party, but somewhat in the nature of an amicus. If you, though, consider that the presence of General Blaskic is necessary, the Trial Chamber is very flexible and very willing, but arrangements would have to be made, and I do not know how quickly General Blaskic would be able to be brought to this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Our position, your Honour, is, since this matter began, this has been a matter in the case of The Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus Tihomir Blaskic. We have never waived our attendance or waived his attendance, despite the fact this is the first hearing we have been given notice of and an opportunity to be present at. Our view is that everybody here but us and the Prosecutor's office is here in the nature of a witness or an amicus. We are the party to this matter other than the Prosecutor's office, we respectfully submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The reason that -- I do not want to speak for Judge Jorda, but the matter was referred first to me, that is the issuance of the subpoena to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the reason that it was referred to me was that Judge Jorda considered that it would be improper for him to handle ex parte the request for the subpoena. Then, of course, when you subsequently filed a subpoena, that was also referred to me, because Judge Jorda, who was the Presiding Judge for the matter that involves General Blaskic, likewise considered that it would be inappropriate for that Trial Chamber, which is seized of the trial of the matter, to handle that issue. So if you had requested, of course, earlier for General Blaskic to be here, I, because I am so flexible and so willing, would have made arrangements. What I am telling you is that we are now all ready -- we are about to begin the hearing and again I do not know how long it would take to bring him. Let me ask and see how long. Do you have any objection to our beginning this matter and then, of course, when General Blaskic arrives, of course we will continue it. I ask you for the same flexibility that I am willing to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last thing that the defence wants to do is inconvenience the many counsel and others who have gathered here this morning. I have vigorously protested since either late January or early February directly to the Registrar and her staff the fact when I first learned of this matter in the newspapers that we were not -- we, the defence, were not given proper notice, not given the opportunity to be heard, and I very much contest that this is a matter other than in the case of the Tribunal Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic, a matter to which he is not only a party but the accused. I am simply not in a position to waive on his behalf his attendance. I would have to speak to him personally in order to make an effective waiver of his attendance. I am sorry, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Mr Hayman, you may have vigorously protested it but you did not vigorously protest it to me or this Trial Chamber. I have never received, nor has this Trial Chamber received, a request that you be present or that General Blaskic be present now. I disagree with your characterisation of the events. If you will have a seat, let me see what can be done to right it. (Pause.) Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The judges have conferred and we consider that this is not a trial of the matter, nor is it a proceeding that in any way would require General Blaskic's presence, but once again in an effort to accommodate you, we will make a determination of whether General Blaskic can be brought to the Tribunal, how long it will take him to be brought, but we will not delay this hearing today pending his arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand and we have stated our position, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I have heard you very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now we were beginning to hear the appearances of counsel and I think we have heard from this side. May I hear regarding the appearances for Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and for the subject of the subpoena directed to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: I am Ivan Simonovic, Ambassador of Croatia to the United Nations, and I represent the Government of Croatia. Together with me is Mr Branko Salaj, Croatian Ambassador to the Netherlands. Legal counsellors: Special legal counsel of the Government of Croatia, Mr David Rivkin; Mrs Katharine Baragona; and Dr Josipovic, an expert on criminal procedural law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Simonovic or Ambassador Simonovic, are you an attorney?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I am here in the capacity of representative of the Government of Croatia and I intend to deliver a statement of the Government of Croatia, and the rest of the proceedings will be presented by special legal counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ambassador Salaj, are you an attorney?

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: No, I am not, and the same that Ambassador Simonovic has expounded goes for me too, except I am not giving a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I certainly did not mean to imply I would hold it against you for not being an attorney. Many people may consider that that is a compliment. I really wanted to know whether when I am perhaps speaking with you and Ambassador Simonovic, I will be speaking to you as an attorney. I gather not. I will be hearing from Mr Rivkin in that regard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And perhaps from Mr Josipovic. Now appearances for Bosnia-Herzegovina. MME VIDOVIC: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, Minister Counsellor in the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in The Hague. I here represent Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GLUMAC
utterances.text: I am Jadranka Slokovic Glumac. I am an attorney at law. I am here as a legal representative of Mr Anto Jelovic, Defence Minister of Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. We also have present amici curiae. May I hear from the amici starting from, I suppose, the left, if you will identify yourself please? Turn on your microphone, Mr Donovan. PROFESSOR DONOVAN: Donald Donovan, Debevoise & Plimpton, New York, on behalf of the Lawyers Committee for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Donovan. PROFESSOR MALANCZUK: My name is Peter Malanczuk. I am Professor of International Law at the University of Amsterdam. PROFESSOR WEDGWOOD: I am Ruth Wedgwood, your Honour, Professor of Law at Yale Law School, Newhaven, Connecticut, US.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIMMERMANN
utterances.text: I am Andreas Zimmermann and I am a Fellow at the Max-Planck Institute of Comparative Public and Public International Law in Heidelberg, Germany. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LJUBANOVIC
utterances.text: I am Professor Vladimir Ljubanovic from the law school in Osijek, and I here act as representative of the Croatian Association of Criminal Science and Practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CONDORELLI
utterances.text: My name is Luigi Condorelli. I am a Professor of International Law at the University of Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. PELLET
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. My name is Alain Pellet. I am Professor for Public International Law at the University of Paris and Institute d'Etudes Politiques. I am a member of the International Law Commission of the United Nations. I appear here both on my personal behalf and for Juristes sans Frontieres. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now before we proceed with the hearing there are certain preliminary matters which need to be resolved that have been raised by letter from Mr Jelanic, who is Head of the Office of Cooperation with the International Tribunal, which I received yesterday, late evening. There are four matters I believe that are raised by that letter, which I asked to be filed with the Registry, since it is a direct communication with the Tribunal. Mr Jelanic is not here, I suppose, to speak to those matters. Mr Rivkin, would you speak to the fourth matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be happy to speak to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Would you speak to the fourth matter or at least according to my enumeration the fourth matter that is raised by that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I presume you are speaking about your possible recuse, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, I am speaking to the request of Croatia that I recuse myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Right. I believe our letter speaks for itself. We just wanted to clarify that we mean no disrespect to your Honour. We are aware of your excellent reputation and distinguished judicial record. We feel, however, in this matter, given the stakes involved not only for the Government of Croatia but for development of international law and the future of this Tribunal, it is important to avoid not only any substantive impropriety but appearance of impropriety. We believe this appearance of impropriety would not even arise if a different jurist rather than the person who issued the subpoenas in the first place was presiding over this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In the letter that was submitted in the next to the last paragraph it stated that: "Finally, Croatia ask that you recuse yourself from participating in this hearing and rendering any decisions on it, since you are the judge who issued the order that is here in issue. Although we, of course, do not doubt your integrity, we believe that both the appearance and substance of fairness and due process require you not to take part in this hearing, or in determining the validity of the subpoena at issue". Mr Rivkin, when I received the letter, I first looked at Rule 15 of our rules of procedure and evidence. Rule 15(A) provides that: "A judge may not sit on a trial or appeal in any case in which he has a personal interest or concerning which he has or has had any association which might affect his impartiality. He shall in any circumstance withdraw and the President shall assign another judge to sit in his place." I first made a determination on my own as to whether or not that rule applied to me, and I do not consider that I have a personal interest in this matter. My only involvement in this matter has been as a sitting judge. Regarding my association, as is referred to in Rule 15 (a), my association has been as follows. First, I signed the subpoena that was addressed to -- the subpoenas that were addressed to Croatia and a high governmental official and Bosnia-Herzegovina and a high governmental official. When Croatia appeared in the person of Ambassador Salaj and challenged the subpoena, I suspended the subpoena at that time and subsequently by an order I requested that the parties brief three issues. I also requested that amicus curiae appear on the issue or issues. I also convened the entire Trial Chamber, even though I felt that I was authorised under our rules to consider the issue. The Prosecutor subsequently filed a motion to lift that suspension of the subpoena. I denied that motion, indicating in the order that the issues would only be considered after the full Trial Chamber resolves the matter, so I do not consider that I have in any way acted improperly, nor do I consider that there is any appearance of impropriety, and therefore I made the decision on my own not to recuse myself. However, Rule 15(b) says a party may apply to the providing judge for a Chamber for the disqualification and withdrawal of the judge of that Chamber upon the above grounds. Since I am the Presiding Judge of this Chamber, I considered it appropriate, and the rule does say or suggest that, if necessary, the Bureau may handle such a request -- I therefore considered it appropriate out of an abundance of caution to refer this matter to the Bureau. I am a member of the Bureau, but I did not participate in its consideration of this issue. The Bureau has considered your request that I recuse myself, and it has issued a Decision which I have been provided, which I would like to read into the record. You have may have a seat, Mr Rivkin. It is as follows: "At the request of Judge McDonald, the Bureau of the Tribunal, consisting of President Antonio Cassese, Judge Adolphus G Karibi Whyte, Judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald and Judge Claude Jorda, met this morning at 9am to consider the request of the Republic of Croatia for Judge McDonald to recuse herself from participating in today's hearing before Trial Chamber II relating to the power of the Tribunal to issue subpoena duces tecum to a sovereign state and from rendering any decision on the matter. The Bureau asked Judge McDonald to state her position, following which she retired and the Bureau deliberated in her absence. After duly considering the issue of recusation, and pursuant to Article 15 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Bureau has unanimously decided to reject the Croatian request for recusation on the following grounds: 1. When the subpoena issued to the Republic of Croatia by Judge McDonald on 15th January 1997 was challenged by the Republic of Croatia in the hearing of 19th February 1997, Judge McDonald, sitting as a sole judge, decided to suspend the subpoena and subsequently invited the parties to address her on matters relating to the power of the Tribunal to issue such a subpoena. 2. On 14th March 1997 Judge McDonald decided to refer the matter to the full Chamber. By deciding not to pronounce on the issue by herself, but in the full Chamber she clearly showed her intention to elicit a full deliberation by the three judges of the Chamber. Consequently, even if one were to argue that her decision to issue the original subpoena might influence her views -- which the Bureau does not believe -- the fact that the matter is now pending before the full Chamber must dispel any doubt in the matter. The question at issue will be deliberated in full by three judges, and any one of them is entitled to append a separate or a dissenting opinion. 3. Subsequently, when the Prosecutor filed a motion for the re I be statement of the subpoena, Judge McDonald, as Presiding Judge of the Chamber, decided to defer ruling on that motion, pending determination of the issues by the full Chamber of the question of the Tribunal's authority to issue such subpoenas. By so acting, Judge McDonald clearly proved herself to be unbiased and to act with full judicial propriety. 4. The Bureau would also like to stress that the decision by Judge McDonald to invite amici curiae to file briefs on this matter clearly shows that she is willing to have the Chamber hear as many legal views as possible, so as to enable the Chamber to reach a proper determination of the matter. This, the Bureau believes, bears testimony to the absolute impartiality and integrity of Judge McDonald. In light of the above, the Bureau, in the absence of Judge McDonald, unanimously decides that Judge McDonald is not precluded by Rule 15(a) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence from participating in the hearing, for she has no personal interest in the case, nor any association with the case which might affect her impartiality." That is signed by Antonio Cassese, President of the Tribunal. I think that disposes of the matter. I apologise for the late beginning of these proceedings and apologise for the time that has been spent in my stating my views regarding the request that I recuse myself as well as reading the decision of the Bureau, but I think that it is important again there is no appearance even of impropriety and we need to proceed with the hearing. Mr Jelanic is not here today, but may I remind Croatia, as well as all of the parties, that communications with this Tribunal, when there is an on-going case, are to be made with the Registry. Letters should not be sent to individual judges, because that, in my judgment at least, would constitute ex parte contact. Such ex parte contact would not only be improper; it would definitely be an appearance of impropriety, and so may I suggest in the future you communicate with the Registry with respect to matters that are pending before this Trial Chamber. Now, you had three other matters, or Mr Jelanic did, that were raised in this letter to me, which I filed with the Registry. Excuse me just one minute. (Pause). I have received word that General Blaskic with be brought to the Tribunal at 2 o'clock, some time between 2 o'clock and 2.30. Judge Jan has reiterated to me the proposition that this is not a trial. As a matter of fact, the issue that we are -- the issues that we are seized with do not directly relate to the request for the issuance of a subpoena by counsel for Blaskic. What is presently before this Chamber is the subpoena that was issued to Croatia and to Bosnia-Herzegovina and the two other -- and the two high officials mentioned in that subpoena. There has been no subpoena signed by this Trial Chamber, nor any judge. Mr Hayman, General Blaskic will be here at 2 o'clock. We will now proceed with the hearing. First, we still have three other issues that we need to resolve. Sorry. The first issue, if you want to go back to the letter, and perhaps at this rate, Mr Hayman, we may not begin the hearing until 2 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I promise to be very brief, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. The first issue in your letter says -- I will read it: "Croatia strongly objects to the timing of this hearing and to the fact that it was accorded only 11 days to make written response to the very lengthy and detailed brief filed by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor has had literally months to prepare and refine its position in this matter. Croatia should have had a reasonable period of at least 30 days to prepare its response. Accordingly Croatia will participate in the hearing on 16th only under protest." Would you like to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are obviously participating in the hearing. We think it is a very important hearing. We are trying to state for the record that we would have liked to have more time to prepare. We know that the matter of a subpoena being issued has been with us for a long time, but speaking as a lawyer, it would have been enormously useful to have a longer time to prepare detailed responses to the legal arguments raised by the Prosecutor. I believe that 11 days is most unusual in matters of that nature. 30 days or 60 days certainly would have been appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I may ask the Prosecutor to respond to this, but on March 7th, 1997 I entered an order asking the parties to brief the issues by April 1st. I looked at the calendar yesterday. I believe I counted 24 days. In any case I entered the matter on March 7th. Briefs were to be entered by April 1st, with reply briefs, if any, by any party, to be filed by April 11th, which is clearly within 30 days. I also requested the submission of amicus briefs by April 7th. I cannot speak to how long the Prosecutor has been preparing its brief or how long it has had. I can tell you, however, that I requested the submission of briefs on March 7th, and asked that the briefs by all parties be filed by April 1st, with reply briefs to be filed by April 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just be permitted to make one point, it is our view, and I do not mean to get into substance at this time, that there is no sufficient authority in international law for issuance of such a subpoena against a sovereign state. Therefore it would have been enormously useful for us to see precisely the legal case made by the prosecution prior to responding. This is a little different than the regular brief and reply brief situation that we have had. As far as the amici briefs are concerned, we got some of those just last night. It is a very compressed timetable on a very important matter of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Did you file the reply brief by April 11th?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: We have, your Honour, a very short reply brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As Mr Hayman has very forcefully pointed out, although the issues that we are now concerned with relate to the propriety of the issuance of a subpoena, there is pending before the other Trial Chamber a matter which involves General Blaskic. General Blaskic has been in custody in excess of 16 months I do believe. Mr Hayman, can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It has been a full year, your Honour. It has been 12 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: 12 months. Even though that is not a matter that this Chamber is concerned with, that is a matter that is being handled by the other Trial Chamber, that was a consideration in my mind when I suspended the subpoena and requested briefing, because I am concerned about the passage of time, even though it does not relate -- even though it is not a matter that is pending before this Trial Chamber, but I hear what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, just to help expedite matters, we would be content with an opportunity to file a substantive reply brief as specified further on in this letter to help cure some of the difficulty. Again it seems to us, given the importance of this issue certainly not in this case but to future international law, that would be entirely appropriate. If you could see your way to rule favourably on that, I would be quite content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I like the way you put that, because in the third point, I suppose, in Mr Jelanic's letter, he does not exactly put it that way. He does not say "if the Trial Chamber can see fit to allow for the filing of additional briefs. " What he says is: "Croatia reserves to itself the right to submit additional written materials". I think that you put it very well and that is a matter that we will consider after we hear the submissions of all the parties. If the Trial Chamber determines that it is either required or it will benefit the Trial Chamber in resolving this issue, we, of course, will allow for additional briefs or submissions to be made, but that is a matter that is left to the decision of the Trial Chamber and not the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I want to thank your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then the second point that was raised in the letter relates to the format of the proceedings. In the letter Mr Jelanic states: "In addition, Croatia objects to the fact that it has not been informed well enough in advance of the hearing of the format the proceeding will take. As a matter of basic fairness and due process, it is incumbent on any court to establish the order of speaking, the time allotted to each side, whether the parties will be expected to respond to questions from the bench, and what form rebuttal argument will take. Croatia has not been informed of these matters with sufficient specificity and amount of detail in a timely manner." Do you wish to elaborate on that, Mr Rivkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, very briefly. It would have been useful for us to know indeed how the rebuttals would take -- in what form they will take place. For example, we were informed last night that we would not be allowed directly to question the amici. That is indeed a reasonable proposition, but it would have been useful to know that a little bit in advance. For example, we still do not know, when the Prosecutor in the second round is going to make some additional points, whether we would be able to talk directly to the Prosecutor or we have to address ourselves to the court. We are not questioning your ability to set your procedures for the court room. It is pretty plenary. Again it would be useful in our preparation to know what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: This is a judicial proceeding. I have presided over a trial that lasted, what, seven months, I guess, and also we at this Trial Chamber considered many motions that were filed in another matter that is pending. Those matters were heard in open court. We have received motions and arguments by counsel dozens of times. If counsel were familiar, either by observing the proceedings or by enquiring, they would know how this Presiding Judge conducts hearings on motions. However, Ambassador Salaj requested by a telephone call to my secretary -- which I referred to our legal officer once again, to avoid any ex parte contact -- he requested a meeting with the Chamber, and we met on April 7th with Ambassador Salaj and another representative from the Embassy, and the Prosecution was present, and we then discussed basically what is the obvious, and that is the moving party goes first. We then hear from the responding party. Now, we will hear, however, from amici. We also discussed how much time would be allotted. Ambassador Salaj said a decision had not been made as to who would appear for Croatia. I have asked him to please advise me at his convenience but please no later than Monday. I asked the parties how much time they thought they would need for the presentation of their arguments. I suggested 45 minutes for each party, but, as I indicated, we are very flexible and willing to hear from the parties as long as they are providing us with something new and not repeating their arguments. I do not understand, Mr Rivkin. This is a judicial proceeding. This is not anything else other than a judicial proceeding and we have had many judicial proceedings. We have considered motions and heard arguments from counsel. We are proceeding in the same basis, but I did meet with Croatia at their request but in the presence of the prosecution and we discussed these matters. I do not think you will have a problem. You are a lawyer. You have appeared in court before. We will proceed very carefully, cautiously and give you enough time. I am satisfied at the end of day and tomorrow you will be satisfied at least you will have had an opportunity to fully state your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think that covers the four matters that you raised in your letter; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. Prosecutor, I have not asked you if you wish to respond to any of these discussions with Mr Rivkin. I have not asked Mme Vidovic, nor have I asked Miss Glumac. If any of you at this point wish to respond to those matters that have been raised, you may. I am not encouraging you, and I am not even suggesting that you need to, but if you wish to, you may. Having heard nothing, we will then proceed. We will proceed now today by hearing first from the Prosecutor. We will then hear the submission from the Defence, and I believe a representative from the Registry, or perhaps the legal officer, Miss Featherstone, has spoken with Mr Hayman regarding time that he night need. We will then hear from the Republic of Croatia. We will then hear from Bosnia-Herzegovina and we will then here from Miss Glumac. We will then hear from the amici and then, of course, there will be time for rebuttal on the part of the prosecution, as well as any replies from Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina or Miss Glumac as well as Mr Hayman, if he still wishes to be present. With respect to the amici, I understand from the Registry that there is a question regarding their availability for tomorrow. May I ask the amici whether there are any who are unable to appear tomorrow, should this hearing last that long? PROFESSOR DONOVAN: I am unlikely to be able to be here tomorrow, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Mr Donovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MALANCZUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have lectures tomorrow. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What do you think your students would say about your absence. We will let you go. I have taught as well. I think you need to be there. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIMMERMANN
utterances.text: I have to fly out tonight because I have to take a lecture tomorrow at a conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You are Mr Zimmermann.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIMMERMANN
utterances.text: Right. PROFESSOR CONDORELLI: I am obliged to leave today because I have to go back to Geneva, because I teach tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is Mr Condorelli.

utterances.speaker: MR. PELLET
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that this morning I was talking with you about this and I could stay until the middle of the afternoon but not any later than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, this is a matter that has the primary interest, I suppose, of the parties, and that is the Prosecution, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Miss Glumac as well as the interests of Mr Hayman. We will do what we can to accommodate amici. We have advised you that we would allot fifteen minutes with some flexibility to respond to questions from the Trial Chamber, but I think that we will be able to hear the direct presentations of the prosecution as well as the direct presentations from Croatia before it is time for the five of you to leave. So we will do our best to accommodate you, but please keep in mind that we have invited you as friends of the court and our first obligation is to the parties. We appreciate your being here and have read your briefs. We will do what we can. Now, having, said all of that, Madam Prosecutor, would you like to begin with your presentation? . Presentation by JUSTICE ARBOUR. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Thank you, your Honour. If I may, on the last issue that was raised with respect to the order of presentation in the spirit of flexibility that you have demonstrated this morning, I wish to state that the prosecution would have no objection to disruption of the order of presentation to give any of the amici an opportunity to be heard, particularly if their presentation was to be restricted to approximately fifteen minutes. We would be happy to either interrupt our own presentation or defer to your calling on them at any particular point rather than to lose the benefit of their presence. We would be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. JUSTICE ARBOUR: If I may just briefly outline the order of presentation, I will be making opening submissions dealing essentially with the proper framework within which the analysis of these proceedings ought to be conducted, and then Mr Crawford will make submissions dealing with the particular issues dealing with matters of international law. Then I will resume my submissions dealing specifically on interests of states and their national security and on the issue of remedies and proper enforcement procedures for the order that we have sought. So if I may just begin by raising a preliminary matter that I believe has been somewhat touched upon in the issues that were raised in the letter that was sent to you, Judge McDonald, I understand yesterday by Mr Jelanic, I do not want to revisit these issues, but there is a related matter that I would like to raise as a preliminary issue, and that relates to the briefs that have been filed with the court by the Republic of Croatia. As I understand it, there were two briefs that were filed, and I will be referring not to the brief that was filed on April 11th in answer to the Prosecutor's brief, but to the original one which is under cover of April 1st, but, in fact, contains a letter, so the brief is really -- the presentation of it is really in the form of a letter that was addressed to your Honour, Judge McDonald, on, I believe, March 28th, and if I may, I would simply like to read the last two paragraphs of that submission. It reads as follows: "Unless the agenda of the hearing set for April 16, 1997 is taken to apply to all states, i.e. the issue is that of universal applicability of the subpoenas, the Republic of Croatia will not take part in the forthcoming proceedings, nor will it consider itself bound by the decisions reached thereafter." The brief continues as follows: "Let us once again remind you", and this is in a letter addressed to you, Judge McDonald, "of the position of the Republic of Croatia as expressed in the above-mentioned letter of March 26 1997 regarding the participation of the Republic of Croatia at the hearing on April 16 1997, and of the significance of the Tribunal's decision for the future cooperation between Croatia and the International Tribunal." Now, with respect to the first paragraph, the one that refers to the Republic of Croatia reserving the right not to consider itself bound by the decision, I simply wish to submit that whichever way the issues are framed, whichever way the issues are argued, and whichever way the issues are decided, in my submission there can be no question that the Republic of Croatia will be bound by the decision of this Tribunal. As for the second paragraph that I have referred to, I wish to submit that the threat of an unfavourable decision would jeopardise the future cooperation between the Republic of Croatia and the Tribunal is not an appropriate form of argument before this Tribunal and that it should be withdrawn. So this is essentially the preliminary point that I wish to address. In light of what has been covered already this morning, I think there is little need to review the judicial history of these proceedings. They are essentially summarised in the Prosecutor's brief at pages 1-4, and I will simply outline the fact that the Prosecutor obtained the subpoenas duces tecum that are at issue in this matter on January 15th 1997, and that on February 10th, so that is a little over two months ago, the Republic of Croatia challenged the legal authority of the Tribunal to issue these subpoenas. So even though I am certainly not raising any objection to the Prosecution going first on this matter, we are essentially here in a proceedings which is akin to a motion to quash an order that was issued, and the question of the legality of the subpoena was squarely put on the table by the Republic of Croatia on February 10th, and I would have thought by the time they alerted the Tribunal to this issue, they would have had the legal foundation for this position certainly thought through, if not fully articulate in writing. So this, I think, sets the context in which these proceedings arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Actually when an objection was lodged there was perhaps a four-page letter that was submitted and filed stating its legal position. So that I did have. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Yes. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I then suspended, as I have indicated already, the subpoena and we then went forward with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Thank you, your Honour. I do not believe that there is any usefulness in reviewing the judicial history of these proceedings beyond having mentioned the salient point. Essentially the central issue that is before the court today is the question of the legality of an order compelling the production of documents and the attendance of witnesses. In my submission, what is not before the court today is the particular form that that order has been issued under. It has been issued under a form that in my submission is provided for by the rules, but this is not essentially, as I understand the position, attacking the legality of the subpoena duces tecum. It is not an attack on its form but it is an impeachment of the very concept of the capacity of the Tribunal to compel the production of evidence, and I think it is useful to approach the issue in these broad terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be permitted for just one second to state what our position is so that the Chamber is not under any misapprehension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do not think that it is appropriate at this time for you to interrupt the argument. You will have an opportunity when you respond to correct any assertions that may be said. This is not a trial where we are receiving evidence. What we are doing is hearing argument. So when we hear from the Prosecutor regarding its framing of your position, you then may respond and state that that truly is not your position. The same when you state your position; it may be that the prosecution wishes to respond, and you will have an opportunity but without interrupting counsel. You may proceed. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Thank you, your Honour. Therefore, in my submission, the critical issue, the central issue, that is before the Tribunal today is the question of the power of the Tribunal to compel the production of evidence and to require the attendance of witnesses in its effort to allow the parties to get access to evidence that they say is necessary for the factual demonstration of their case at trial. In my submission, therefore, the question is not one of the form that this order could take, although it has been raised certainly by many of the amicus briefs, that the particular form that this order has taken has raised some questions as to whether it is an appropriate type of procedure. Our submissions will be that it is an order that is fully contemplated by the rules, but the essence of the issue is not so much whether this vehicle is the appropriate one, but very much whether the Tribunal has the capacity to compel the production of evidence, including of documentary evidence. I will be developing this argument as to what the true nature of a subpoena is. A subpoena duces tecum is essentially an order to appear. That is the "subpoena" part. It is an order to appear that conveys the sense that the order is compulsory. The addition of the expression "duces tecum" essentially requires the witness not only to attend but to bring forward to the court documents that may then have to be addressed by the witness in giving evidence. If the documents are put forward in their entirety, there is very often no need for the witness actually to attend. If the production of the document is somewhat deficient, insufficient, not complete, the witness may then be called to explain the deficient production or in another way to speak to the question of documentary production. What is also critical, in my submission, to understand and to cast the debate squarely within these parameters is that this is an order for the production of documents that has been sought by the Prosecutor, and a similar order has been sought by the Defence, in the post-indictment phase of the proceedings of the Tribunal. In my submission, this is a critical distinction that I would like to take the court through by pointing to the two different schemes that in my submission govern access by the prosecution to documentary and testimonial evidence. Pre-indictment, that is in the course of the Prosecutor investigating the crimes that are within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, therefore, the statutes contemplated in Article 16 that the Prosecutor is responsible essentially for investigations. Under Article 18, paragraph 2 of the Statute, the Prosecutor is given powers: "The Prosecutor shall have the power to question suspects, victims, witnesses, to collect evidence and to conduct on-site investigations. In carrying out these tasks, the Prosecutor may, as appropriate, seek the assistance of states' authorities concerned." Under Article 29 of the Statute the Prosecutor, in my submission, is then entitled to call upon the states for their -- to call them upon their obligation to cooperate. Article 29 contemplates that: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or an order issued by a Trial Chamber." That includes cooperation with respect to identification, taking of testimony, production of evidence and so on. So in the investigative phase of the proceedings, the Prosecutor is entitled to make requests for assistance to states and is entitled to rely on the duty to cooperate which is expressed in Article 29 of the Statute. This is all pre-indictment, and this entitlement of the Prosecutor is then repeated and reflected and fleshed out, if I may put it this way, in rule 39 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which essentially track the language that I have referred to in the Statute. Under the current practice of the Prosecutor's office, there are literally hundreds of such requests for assistance addressed to various states that are at various stages of compliance. Many are outstanding; many are the subject of protracted discussions with the states concerned, including, in many cases, a request by the state for more specificity and so on. In my submission, none of this is before the court today. We are now in another set of statutory provisions that govern the production of evidence at trial. In my submission, it is critical to properly situate this order that is sought by the Prosecutor and a similar order that is sought by the defence in this post-indictment phase of the Tribunal's proceedings. After an indictment has been confirmed, and this is the case in this particular case that is before the Tribunal, Article 19 of the Statute, Article 19, paragraph 2, provides that: "Upon confirmation of an indictment the judge may, at the request of the Prosecutor, issue such orders and warrants for the arrest, detention, surrender or transfer of persons and any other order as may be required" -- that is a critical point -- "for the conduct of the trial." Post-indictment, both in the pre-trial and the trial phases of the post-indictment process, the orders that are available to the parties, not solely at that point to the Prosecutor, but to the parties are orders that will assist the parties in a thorough presentation of their case to the trial court. Article 20 then continues in this post-indictment phase by providing that: "The Trial Chambers must ensure that the trial is fair and expeditious and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence." Article 15 delegates essentially the rule-making power to the judges in plenary, and we have supplementing the Statute, therefore, under that authority a body of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Article 29 again calls upon state cooperation and makes specific reference to the obligation of states not only to comply with requests for assistance, but specifically to orders issued by a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Article 29 then is not limited to pre-indictment or post-indictment. That is the general Article on cooperation, because included in Article 29 is the duty to execute arrest warrants. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now we are moving into a hybrid or perhaps even over-arching requirement. JUSTICE ARBOUR: The distinction I wish to draw, your Honour, between the pre-indictment and post-indictment proceedings are a way of distinguishing between requests for assistance that are supportive of investigations and in which states have been given by the security counsel the obligation to be cooperative in the Prosecutor's effort to investigate, which is one part, and the obligations of the state that are commensurate to the powers of the court as a criminal court when its trial jurisdiction is engaged after an indictment has been issued, to be given the appropriate means, no longer merely to investigate the possible commission of an offence, but to come to a just, fair and reliable disposition of the allegations, and these powers, in my submission, are powers that are universal in all criminal courts, and I want to wait this order that was sought by the Prosecutor, as a similar order was sought by the defence, to properly wait that order in its post-indictment context, to make it clear that what we are talking about here is not a kind of fishing expedition in the broad base investigations that could be conducted in the pre-indictment phase. When the Prosecutor is given powers to ascertain whether crimes were committed that are within the ambit of the Statute, and by whom -- this is not what is at issue in this case. We are now in the phase in which the parties are given entitlements that will assist them in providing the court with reliable facts upon which to make the determination that it must make, which has, of course, the consequences that we know that could include sentencing a person for life imprisonment, and in my submission this is the proper context in which we have to examine these provisions. Therefore, in my submission the order that was sought by the Prosecutor here is very squarely rooted in Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This will explain the particular form that this order took, although, as I submitted earlier, nothing turns, in my submission, on the fact that it is a subpoena that was sought rather than an order that could have been cast using a different terminology. Rule 54 provides that: "At the request of either party or proprio motu a judge or Trial Chamber may issue such orders, summonses or subpoenas, warrants or transfer orders as may be necessary for the purposes of: (i) an investigation". In my submission that would clearly contemplate a continuing post-indictment investigation, which is entirely appropriate. Considering the indictment standard that is provided for in Rule 47, there is certainly no suggestion there is anything inappropriate in the investigation continuing post-indictment, but in my submission in the investigation that is being contemplated here, the post-indictment one. "Orders that are necessary for the purposes of an investigation, or for the preparation or conduct of the trial." Rule 54 is included in part 5 of the rules, which is entitled "Pre-trial Proceedings", and then follows into the proceedings at trials. Rule 54, therefore, is squarely situated in what in my submission is the power that is not only expressly provided for in the Statute but that is an implied and inherent power universally enjoyed by all criminal courts to compel the production of evidence, to compel testimony and to compel the production of evidence, assuming, of course, and dependent on a determination by the court that the evidence sought is sufficiently relevant, material, probative to be admitted, and is not otherwise caught by some exclusionary rule. That power, in my submission, is universally enjoyed by criminal courts, and the order sought in these proceedings is in substance, and I will address the form later, in substance is an order that belongs to that range of instruments that are at the disposal of the court. Following Rule 64 there are many other provisions of the rule that speak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Following Rule 54, you mean, but before you go on to that, of course the provision is provided for in Rule 54, but where is there a foundation in the Statute? Would you say Article 29 is that foundation? Article 29 seems to be a hybrid in that it provides for cooperation and then what it provides for in terms of the type of cooperation, it includes the production of evidence, which, of course, could be post-trial -- post-indictment, but also the identification and location of persons, which may be pre-indictment, but in any case what I want you to do is to anchor rule 52 to an article in the Statute. Mr Pellet has said in his brief that I found that I had power only in Rule 54. I think it became clear, if the full transcript was read, that there was always a reference to an article in the Statute. So, you tell me, where does Rule 54 have its anchor in the Statute, because obviously when bodies enact rules, even in my system, they cannot legislate. They cannot go beyond the constituent documents. So where in the Statute? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Well, in my submission, certainly Article 29 in itself could be seen as sufficient anchor for that power, but I would certainly like to rely as well on Articles 19 and 20, then go to Article 15, providing for the legality of Rule 54. I say Article 19, because this is the Article -- this is the first Article in the Statute that specifically contemplates that: after an indictment has been confirmed, the Prosecutor now and the accused, in my submission, have access to the court for any order as may be required for the conduct of the trial. It will be my submission that it could not have not been within the contemplation of the Security Council to realise that the conduct of a criminal trial requires the court to equip itself, which it has done by, in part Rule 54 and other rules -- to equip itself with the ability to compel from potentially reluctant third parties the access to testimony or documents that will be necessary for a just, fair and reliable determination of the issues that are put before the Tribunal. So I say, and these are my submissions, that the statutory anchor starts in Article 19 that provides for the post-indictment capacity of the court to make orders for the conduct of the trial, and in my submission this is then followed by Article 20, which again imposes a statutory duty on the court to ensure a fair and expeditious trial. My submission is there cannot be a trial that is fair to either party if the party cannot turn to the court for its assistance in compelling reluctant or potentially reluctant witnesses -- and by witnesses I include witnesses who have access to documents -- if the court could not compel reluctant third parties to produce this evidence for the assistance of the court in coming to a fair, expeditious and reliable determination of the issues. So in my submission Rule 54 is very solidly anchored in Article 19, Article 20 and clearly in the obligation imposed on states in Article 29 to comply in absolutely mandatory language: "States shall comply with orders issued by Trial Chambers". Turning back to Article 19, that includes any order that is required for the conduct of the trial, and in my submission, orders such as this one compelling the production of evidence, be it testimonial evidence or documentary evidence, fall squarely within the powers that a criminal court must enjoy if it will be given the power to preserve the integrity of its final factual conclusions. I would add to that Article 21, which I think is not insignificant in the present context, particularly Article 21, paragraph 4(e), which grants the accused the right: "In determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees." I read (e): "To examine or have examined the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him." In my submission the subpoena, as I stated earlier, is an order for a person to appear as a witness and produce documents to the court. Whichever characterisation one may want to give to that document, if issued in the course of a trial, that is what it is. Documents do not walk into the court room. They can only be presented to the court either pursuant to a seizure following a search warrant, in which case the search officer will testify, present the document and testify to the location where the documents were found, the conditions under which they were found, and will provide the court with information about their circumstances, if I can put it this way. Obviously a search warrant is the most intrusive method of compelling evidence, documentary evidence, to be brought before the court. A somewhat less intrusive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us not get that far in this hearing, please. JUSTICE ARBOUR: In my submission the other method --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is for a later date. JUSTICE ARBOUR: The other method for introducing documentary evidence before the court is the method pursued here, which is issuing an order for a witness to bring the documents before the court and if necessary, to testify as to their authenticity, the locations in which they were found and so on. In this particular case the subpoena was sought pre-trial, but in my submission absolutely nothing turns on that distinction. The critical distinction is that it is post-indictment. Therefore it calls into play Article 29, Article 20, Article 29 and Rule 54. The fact that it was issued pre-trial is merely a matter of convenience. This order was sought by the Prosecutor on January 15th of this year. It should be pretty obvious that it would have been unwise in the extreme for the Prosecutor to wait for trial and issue -- seek the issuance of this subpoena to require the attendance of the two witnesses that are the object of the subpoena, to require their attendance at trial to produce these documents. The fact that it was done prior to trial does not change the proper legal characterisation of what these orders are. They are a court order that is geared to the production of evidence at trial, although they are done in a preliminary matter for expediency's sake, if I can put it this way. In my submission, there is to legal consequence that turns on the fact that they were issued prior to trial. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Pre-trial. Prior to trial. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Prior to trial but post-indictment. In my submission, that is the critical distinction. This brings me to situating these proceedings in their proper criminal law context. In my submission whether a subpoena is a particular force of compellability of witness attendance and production of documents is not the issue. It is perfectly clear from the many submissions that have been made to the court that it is not a vehicle that is known as such in all criminal jurisdictions, and in retrospect it might have been preferable not to alarm potential recipients of that order, but to merely state that this is an order compelling the attendance of a witness and the production of documents, rather than use a terminology that may be seen as containing more than it does. It is simply an order compelling the attendance of the witness, the production of documents, and it conveys that there is a compulsory order, and there is no element of discretion. I will turn to remedies and enforcement after Mr Crawford makes arguments with respect to international law issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just ask you a question regarding your characterisation of the meaning of subpoena. You say it is an order with compulsion. Of course, Croatia would say that it is under penalty -- I do not want to speak for Croatia -- it is not under compulsion but under penalty and it presupposes that the issuing authority has a power then to impose a penalty. You phrased it differently. You have said it is under compulsion. Do you disagree that subpoena means by its very definition under penalty? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Certainly it is terminology -- it's a literal translation of the Latin expression suggests it is not "under pain" -- it is "under the threat of penalty", but in my submission this is giving way too literal an interpretation to this particular vehicle for the compellability of evidence. The penalty that is being contemplated is simply a means of enforcement. Ultimately what the court seeks is not to punish recalcitrant witnesses. What the court seeks is to make them attend. So the threat of unpleasant consequences in some cases may be felt more strongly than in others by some of the potential witnesses, but ultimately the object is to secure the attendance of the witness or obtain the documents. There is no goal in the punishment by itself. This is not a criminal sanction that has any other purpose but to give teeth to the power of the court to secure the attendance of the witness and the production of documents. So the fact that the penalty may be unavailable either because, for instance, in the case of a fine, the witness has no money, in my submission is totally immaterial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is an empty threat. JUSTICE ARBOUR: It is not an empty threat in my submission in the case of individuals. It has indeed rather serious consequences if there is a defiance of a court order in the case of an individual, and in my opinion the fact that this particular statutory framework may not contemplate a penalty in the traditional sense, a fine, for instance, being imposed on a state, does not in any way detract from the legally binding character of the order. The fact that it may not be either wise or feasible to impose, for instance, a nominal fine on a state in my submission does not change the fact that a state can be legally bound to comply. The unpleasantness of the consequences may be felt differently by an individual, as they are by a corporation, a corporate entity or a state, but in my submission it does not change the legally binding character. Obviously compliance is made more difficult when there is an absence of access to a penalty that would serve as an encouragement. I will certainly concede that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think Mr Condorelli would say the problem is not with the thing but with what the thing is called. So perhaps the opposition to the use of a document called a subpoena is because it is not something that is known in civil law and because traditionally in common law it carries with it the penalty of a fine and imprisonment, but that is not the only interpretation. The problem really is what the thing is called, but the thing could have different consequences, or no? You tell me. JUSTICE ARBOUR: In my submission, the methods of compelling the production of evidence and the testimony of witnesses vary greatly, particularly between legal systems that have a common law root and civilian legal systems. I will concede that, but it is absolutely crystal clear that even in systems that do not use that particular technique, invariably all criminal courts that purport to hold fair criminal trials put at the disposal of the judicial organ the capacity to access, either directly or by putting tools in the hands of the parties -- to access the evidence, be it testimonial or documentary, that is essential for a reliable disposition of the case. Whether this is done by giving a juge d'instuction very broad powers, for instance, of accessing himself or herself that evidence or whether it is done by equipping the parties with the capacity to bring this evidence into court, it is a wide variation in procedures, but it does not detract from the empowerment that all criminal courts have in one form or another to compel or to access -- I will put it this way, because either it done on their own motion or by compelling others to do it -- to compel the production of factual information that is necessary for a reliable and fair disposition of the case. So the fact that this particular technique is not available in legal systems, where most of the factual information is collected by a judicial officer, such as a juge d'instruction, who has enormous coercive powers himself, akin to a search warrant, where there is a more proactive judicial direct access to the evidence, or whether it is done by a court ordering witnesses to attend trial, in my submission does not change the fundamental characteristic. Why this procedure was chosen here by the prosecution is because that is the one that is the most easily traceable in the language of the rules. The reference to a subpoena is contained in Rule 54, so it was certainly an available mechanism, and I will be making submissions, if you will allow me, a little later on the question of remedies and enforcements that will allow me to link that particular procedure to Rule 77, but I am ahead of myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Rule 54 was amended on January 30th, 1995. In the annual report it states that it was amended to include the use of subpoenas: "... to improve the clarity, consistency and completeness of the rule". In your brief you say for clarifying. Actually that is not the full statement. The annual report says: "... to improve the clarity, consistency and completeness." Is it your position that the Statute gives the Tribunal the power to issue a subpoena explicitly, or are you saying that it is implicit in the power to issue orders? JUSTICE ARBOUR: It is clear there is no explicit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Or are you saying it is the inherent power that the Tribunal has, regardless of a specific reference in the Statute? JUSTICE ARBOUR: In my submission, if nothing else, it would have to form part of the inherent powers of a criminal court. There would be no doubt that a mechanism would have to be designed by the court itself to allow it to get access to the evidence that is necessary for a fair disposition of the case. It seems to me that there is no legal system purporting to hold a fair criminal trial that would be able to afford the risk of having its factual conclusion undermined by a third party withholding information and then releasing it after the court has reached a decision, to undermine the reliability of the product. Whichever means are used to achieve that purpose, either the court will equip itself or will equip the parties, or will use another judicial officer, but ultimately a criminal court, which is formally required to make a conclusion of fact, either beyond a reasonable doubt or on some equivalent very high standard of proof -- there is no criminal court that can discharge that mandate without having -- without being equipped to make sure that no information can be withheld from the court, subject, of course to relevance, materiality and exclusionary rules that in the end still serve the interests of justice. So, in my submission, if nothing else, it would have been implicit that an inherent power of that nature existed when the Security Council created a criminal court -- it is the only international criminal court, but as not just a judicial organ but that type of judicial organ -- absent anything else, in my submission, it would have been implicit that it has such powers. I say the case is much easier than that, because the Statute contains language perfectly consistent with that in the Articles that I have submitted earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That speak to orders. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Orders that are necessary for the conduct of the trial, the trial having to be fair and expeditious and the accused having rights to compel the attendance of witnesses in support of its position and so on. So the seeds, I think, of that power are clearly founded in the Statute. If I may make one final --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So the power is inherent but also provided by the Statute. JUSTICE ARBOUR: In my submission it is express. In a Statute -- let us be very clear -- that contains 34 Articles -- I mean, this Statute was never meant to be expressed to that level. When a Statute creates a criminal court and gives the judges of that court the power to make orders that are necessary for the conduct of a fair trial, in my submission, that is an express power of compellability, of testimonial and documentary evidence. What form that power will take varies greatly, depending on the particular structure of different legal systems, but it is unquestionable, in my submission, that that is what is contemplated by the giving of that kind of powers to a judge presiding over a criminal trial that purports to be fair, efficient, effective and that will produce a reliable conviction or acquittal. If I may just make one final submission with respect to this terminology of subpoena, rule 98 provides that: "A Trial Chamber may order either party to produce additional evidence at trial." Then it says: "It may itself summon witnesses and order their attendance." It is my submission that it would have made no difference had this rule said: "It may itself order a subpoena to witnesses and order their attendance." What is contemplated -- and in my opinion it would not be a useful exercise to try to distinguish between, in common law jurisdictions, what is the difference between a summons and a subpoena -- in my submission it makes no difference. What this speaks to is this fundamental compellability power, which is then exercised to the very end prior to the final factual determination. The court then has this residual power in Rule 98 perfectly well rooted, in my submissions, in the Statute, in Article 19, 20 and 29, to ensure that all relevant material necessary, factual information, has been put at its disposal for a fair determination of the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you one moment, and it is very difficult to separate your position that the Tribunal has the power to issue an order with compulsion with the question of remedies, because it may be that we have the power to issue an order or a request, but as soon as we state that we have the power to issue a subpoena, it is certainly implied that will be with compulsion exercised with the issuing party. That is when we get into a problem. Now is that something that Mr Crawford is going to address. Do you understand what I am saying? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Everything you have said so far is not even contested. That is there is the power to issue orders and requests, but when you speak of orders with compulsion, particularly if you are talking about compulsion issued by the issuing party, that is when we get into some disagreement. JUSTICE ARBOUR: I am sorry. I think I misunderstood. When you say issued by the issuing party, the order is a court order, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is true, but the order that is issued with compulsion, a subpoena, the party that issues it, that is the court, then has the power to determine appropriate sanctions. It may be that you want to leave that aside and say that at this point what you are talking about is the power in the Statute and the inherent power to make -- for a criminal court to issue orders that must be compiled with, period. Then the issue of whether or not it is up to the court or whether the court has the power to compel compliance is an entirely different issue, which may relate to remedies. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Yes. I may answer very briefly, but, if I may, I think I could make a more cogent argument on the whole enforcement issue after Professor Crawford situates the debate in the international context, but in answer to your question I will say that, if I am correct up to this point, that what we are talking about is the power of a court to compel testimonial and documentary evidence, it is implicit, in my opinion, that compellability has to have some means of enforcement, and my submission will be that Rule 77, given a proper interpretation that is meant to render the intent of the Statute effective, has all the components that make it permissible for the court to use that mechanism to compel the attendance of the witness and the production of documents by that witness under the threats of penalties that are contemplated by that provision, but I may return -- unless you want full submissions on that point at this stage, what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is it necessary and essential, though, for the Tribunal to have the power to not only issue an order but to at the same time have the power to compel compliance with the order? Is it necessary and essential for the Tribunal to have that second power, that is to order -- to compel compliance with that order, or would resort to the Security Council to enforce, so to speak, that order not also be as effective, particularly considering that the Security Council has more power, at least in its arsenal of effective measures, than Rule 77 has of a US $10,000 fine and six months' imprisonment? The Security Council has some pretty powerful measures at their disposal. So is it not as effective for the Security Council to act than for this Tribunal to say 6 months, 10,000 dollars fine. JUSTICE ARBOUR: In my submission, these remedies are cumulative. They are not exclusive of each other. The weight of the Security Council may be brought to bear to a recalcitrant state, that is a state against whom a legally binding order has been issued, and who is not complying. In my submission the proper avenue for the Tribunal is to turn to the Security Council or frankly to public opinion -- these proceedings are public -- and that is the end of the road in terms of the enforcement of the compellability powers of the court, but in my submission it would be most inconvenient and certainly not contemplated by the Statute that when the court issues a summons to a witness that, if witness does not appear, that the court would then turn to the Security Council with a list of names of persons who are not complying. This is why, in my submission, Rule 77 is perfectly consistent with the power of the court to control its own proceedings and to enforce its absolutely unambiguous powers to compel the production of evidence from natural persons, persons who can be physically brought before the court. I will be returning to that point, if I may, later, but in my submission the two are not mutually exclusive on this point. If I may then just summarise my introductory remarks, it is, in my submission, expressed under the Statute and implied in the creation by the Security Council of a criminal court that the court has to have the power to compel testimonial and documentary evidence. What Mr Crawford will address is whether or not the international character of this criminal court in any way departs from the power that all criminal courts enjoy in all jurisdictions that have a mandate similar to this one. I will be returning to my submissions on national security and remedies after Mr Crawford. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: One minute, Mr Crawford: (Pause). If I may speak to the Prosecutor, you had indicated very kindly in your opening remarks that you would defer your argument -- not your time -- at least interrupt your argument so that the amici who have time constraints could present their argument. After conferring, the judges think that it may be appropriate now, Mr Crawford, to begin to hear from the amici who have time constraints. We will then recess for lunch at 1 o'clock, and return at 2.30. We do not need an hour and a half to eat, but there are other parties who need to make arrangements and need that time. Then we would, I suppose, conclude with the five amici who have to leave, Mr Crawford, if you do not mind, and then we would hear from you. Is that acceptable? Okay. Very good. Now, Mr Pellet, we have prepared a list here of order of amici, and we had wanted to hear, because of time constraints, I guess, from Mr Pellet, then Mr Condorelli, both of whom have a time problem, and then we will hear from the other amici who have time problems. Is there any objection to that, Mr Rivkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: None, your Honour. You may proceed as you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Miss Vidovic, Miss Glumac? MME VIDOVIC: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Pellet, come forward. Presentation by PROFESSOR PELLET

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Pellet, I read your submission. We all read your submission. I appreciate it. It was very good. I have a question regarding the issuance of subpoenas to individuals, subpoena duces tecum to individuals. Is it your position that the Tribunal may only issue a subpoena to an individual in his personal capacity or is it your position, as you later take, at least on page 16, I think, that the Tribunal may address a subpoena to an individual even if exercising the official function, and that would bind them independently of whether they are agents -- whether they are state agents? So would you tell me what your position is regarding the power of the Tribunal to issue a subpoena to an individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. PELLET
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you do not mind, I take my brief. Your Honour, my position, I think, is rather clear and rather firm. The Tribunal and all its components can address a subpoena to an individual as an individual. If that person also has official functions, that person cannot refuse to appear before the Tribunal or to execute its order on the pretext that he is carrying out official functions. However, if the Tribunal desires to hear a person not as an individual but in his official capacity, at that point my feeling is that the Tribunal must consider that the individual is actually the state and the objections against the subpoena that I have can therefore be fully expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that we would call an individual -- let us say he is a Minister of Defence, for example -- and ask that he produce certain documents? That Minister then could not object on the pretext that he is carrying out official functions, but if we are calling him because of his official capacity, then actually that would be a subpoena addressed to the state? If that is your position, we would typically not have an interest in an individual who is a custodian of documents in an official capacity. That would be the only reason that a subpoena would be addressed to him, unless, of course, the Prosecutor or the defence wish to issue a subpoena to a witness or some person who is not connected with the state and does not hold documents in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PELLET
utterances.text: I believe that you, your Honour, understood what I had in mind. I believe that if an individual is, for instance, Minister of Defence, but because of his background he learned about certain things which might be of interest to the Tribunal, and might be of interest to the Tribunal as a witness, even if he is a Minister of Defence, which would not be a problem for the Tribunal in that case, and therefore I continue at that point to continue to state that the Tribunal is fully entitled to order him as an individual, Mr X or Mr Y, can order him to appear before it, and in no way can this individual hide behind his official responsibilities. What disturbs, me -- if you permit me to make a comment -- what disturbs me in the orders you issued, and which are the reason for all of these proceedings here, is that you ordered the appearance of two Ministers of Defence of two sovereign states, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, but, having named them -- and I think that things would have been much more simple and that we would have better understood whether you were addressing yourself as to an individual or as an organ of the state if you had either said: "I want Mr X or Mr Y to appear" -- that would have been clear that it was Mr X or Mr Y; the fact he was Minister of Defence would not be important -- or to say: "I want the Minister of Defence to appear." At that point things would also have been clear. You wanted them as a Minister, as Minister of Defence, and I think then the question would have been posed differently. I think that Mrs Arbour did not convince me, because she is not making those distinctions, which to me seem to be basic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So what you are advocating is that every individual has two obligations, one to his own state and the other to the Tribunal, and his obligation to his own state is subordinate to his obligation to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PELLET
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I do not think that that is really what I have in mind. What I have in mind is that any individual vis-a-vis the Tribunal must respond to the orders which he receives, and I make no distinction in that respect whether we are speaking about an individual acting as an individual or as one who is working or acting as the representative of the state. I would like to make a distinction there but you are not asking me this question -- I would like to make a distinction when it comes to knowing what orders can be addressed to him, and I think the order given to him is different depending on whether the individual is acting as an individual or whether he is acting as a representative of the state, but I make no distinction at all between the fact that individuals have to appear before you, just as states must respect the orders that are addressed to them, but does it mean that the Tribunal can issue any type of order to any individual?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How would you phrase -- as an internationalist rather than a criminalist how would you, as you say in your brief, phrase the subpoena?
