We would say that the same presumption applies in relation to this Tribunal as a subordinate organ of the Security Council created to perform a particular function. The members of the United Nations, by authorising the Security Council to do various things, including the creation of this Tribunal, and the Security Council by, pursuant to that authorisation, entrusting certain functions to this Tribunal, with the attendant duties and responsibilities, must have clothed it with the competence required to enable those functions to be effectively discharged. Of course, that is not to say that the provisions of the Statute are to be interpreted ad libitum. It is not to say that the Tribunal is free to reach any conclusion whatever, but it is to say that the Tribunal must apply basic principles of the interpretation of the Charter and of instruments made pursuant to it in the way indeed which the International Court would do. We see the application of that principle in a context very similar to that of the present, with one important exception, to which I will return, in the United Nations Administrative Tribunal case, which is in the same volume of Prosecutor's authorities at tab 12. The question there was whether the General Assembly could create a subordinate judicial body with the authority to make binding decisions as between the United Nations and staff members on questions relating to the employment of members of staff. Having concluded that under its Statute the United Nations Administrative Tribunal was authorised to act as a judicial body and not merely an advisory body, the next question for the International Court in that case was whether the decisions of the Tribunal were binding on the United Nations, that is binding on the General Assembly, so that the General Assembly had no legal alternative but to comply with the decisions. The Charter said nothing on that question. It had simply to be inferred from the structure of the Charter. The International Court said that -- this is at page 57: "The power to establish the Tribunal to do justice as between the organisation and the staff members was essential to ensure the efficient working of the secretariat, etc."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you referring to these volumes? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It is Prosecutor's Volume 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I cannot find the paging on here. There is no paging on here. PROFESSOR: CRAWFORD: The tabs do not appear on the side. They have to be divined. It is tab 12. You can only tell if you reach it. It is a bit like the suburbs of London. One only knows one is in them when one gets there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Continue with the case and then I have a question about it. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It is pages 57 and 58 of the UN Administrative Tribunal decision. The court said first that capacity to establish this Tribunal as an judicial body arises by necessary attainment, because it is necessary in order to enable the tasks afforded to -- entrusted to the United Nations to be carried out, but this is the crucial point. It was then said: "Well, fine. You can establish a subordinate tribunal of a judicial character, but you cannot make its decisions binding on the United Nations. It would be sufficient to make them, as it were, advisory, but you cannot take the next step." The court then said in response to that argument on page 58 that whether to take the next step was a matter for the General Assembly. The Charter was not to be restrictively construed so only what was minimally necessary to achieve the aims was conferred. It was to be construed so as to grant the relevant political body the discretion to decide what was appropriate within the parameters laid down by the Charter itself. As the court said at the bottom of page 58: "The precise nature and scope of the measures by which the power of creating a Tribunal was to be exercised was a matter for determination by the General Assembly alone." We would say the same thing was true in the context of the Security Council here. So that is the basic principle of interpretation. Your Honour, you said you had a question, and perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The question -- relating to this case, of course, they say that -- it is contended there is no need to go so far and that an implied power can only be exercised to the extent that the particular measure under consideration can be regarded as absolutely essential, and so was it not essential for this body to make binding decisions regarding claims of staff members? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, the court proceeded on the basis that you could have resolved that problem by something less than a decision binding on the General Assembly itself. Whether or not that was an appropriate judgment is a question, but the opinion proceeds on the basis that the need could have been met by a body which made decisions binding on the staff member and, as it were, strongly persuasive so far as the General Assembly was concerned, but not absolutely binding. This was in the context where the General Assembly was seeking to refuse to appropriate the money that would be necessary to comply with an award. What the court said was not: "No, you are wrong in your judgment about what was necessary". It said: "No, the proper principle of interpretation is to interpret the Charter so that it gives a discretion on the question of appropriateness to the relevant political body". We are not to adopt narrow interpretations of what is necessary. Provided it is within the framework of the Charter and in conformity with its purposes and principles, then the power is to be treated as conferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Where does this necessity argument end? As we would say, is it a slippery slope? Is it really necessary and essential -- I think in your first argument you say "necessary or essential" and in your second argument you say it is "necessary and essential". Is it truly necessary and essential that the Tribunal be able to enforce its orders with respect to the production of documents? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, there are two different questions. There is the question whether the Security Council has the power to do something, and there is the question how it has exercised that power. The decisions that I have cited relate to the question of the exercise of power by the political body itself, which is not constrained but is governed by the principle of effectiveness within the framework of the Charter. So you then have to look at the text, the actual Statute,, to see what is conferred, but there is no principle of limitative interpretation. There is no principle that less power is conferred, because, for example, it could not have been conferred, than was necessary to achieve the effective implementation of a particular measure, on the assumption, of course, that that measure is itself authorised by the Charter. In other words, if the Security Council creates a criminal trial body, which is going to conduct -- and this is the words of the Security Council Resolution -- effective prosecution of particular crimes, then one can infer that all of the powers that are necessary in order to enable the effective prosecution of crimes have been given, subject to the proper interpretation of the Statute. Now, of course, there are some limitations, both limitations at the level of jurisdiction and, as we will say, limitations at the levels of appropriateness of exercise of the powers, but there is no limitation of restrictive interpretations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: One amicus suggests our powers should be narrowly constrained because the Security Council acted as an enforcement measure. I believe, and I do not remember which one -- PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Professor Malanczuk, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In any case, my question really is: considering this is the first time that the Security Council has created an ad hoc tribunal, relying on its powers under Chapter 7, it seems to me that perhaps an argument can be made that we should very carefully look at what was given the Tribunal, given the fact it is an extraordinary, perhaps, exercise of those powers -- if not extraordinary, at least this is the first time it has been exercised. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Unprecedented. That is the better way to look at it. If any case, if it is unprecedented, should we not be very careful to not exceed the powers that are given to us, and if in doubt as to whether we have the power, approach it from a very narrow and cautious approach, given the first time the Security Council has done this. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: If something is to be done the first time, one might say it is best it is done effectively. The question in the end is: what do the words mean? The intention of the Security Council was to give this court an effective trial jurisdiction in respect of the crimes specified. As with all principles of interpretation, there is a limit. There is a point beyond which it cannot be pressed. As my submissions develop, I will suggest some of those limitations, but there is no a priori principle of restrictive interpretation if that conflicts with the basic purpose that this Tribunal should be an effective trial mechanism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Why do you consider that it was the intention of the Security Council to create a Tribunal that would be effective? PROFESSOR: CRAWFORD: Because of the word "effective" in the relevant Resolutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is a good answer. Could it not have been more effective if we were given police power? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: As I have already said, the point cannot be pressed beyond a certain limit. The question in the end is still: what do the words of the Statute mean? Perhaps I might turn to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Anyway, your position is that the ability to issue subpoenas that have penalties attached to them, at least so far as high governmental officials are concerned, is necessary and essential to the exercise of this Tribunal's judicial functions. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: I did not yet say that, your Honour. If I can expand on my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You have not got to that. That is in your brief. In any case it is necessary and essential and -- PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: All I have said so far is that one applies the principle of effectiveness against the background of the cases that I have mentioned in the interpretation of the actual language of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. You can develop your argument. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Turning to the character of the Tribunal, this is of critical importance in the way in which its powers are to be exercised, and that applies in a number of ways. The first point to note, of course, and this is not disputed, that the Tribunal is an international tribunal. It is not a national court in any respect. It is a international body governed by international law. It is a very special and unprecedented sort of international tribunal in two respects. First of all, it is a criminal tribunal, which is entrusted with the task of determining the guilt or innocence of individuals in respect of the most serious crimes in the calendar. That already gives it a special character, as the Prosecutor has mentioned. The second point to note about the Tribunal, which is also unprecedented in the modern period, is that it has territorial jurisdiction. It has territorial jurisdiction under Article 8 of the statute. That territorial jurisdiction is associated with primacy over national courts under Article 9, paragraph 2. So it is a very unusual creature. Its unusual character is associated with the requirement that it should conduct effective trials of individuals in respect of serious crimes. It is an international court with territorial jurisdiction over the whole territory of a former state and with primacy over the courts of that territory. It is true that it also has primacy over the courts of other territories, but it is the combination of territorial jurisdiction and primacy which is quite distinctive. It would be very odd if a criminal court required to conduct effective trials and which had both territorial jurisdiction and primacy in respect of the territory where the alleged crimes were said to have taken place lacked the power to give effect to its jurisdiction. So that reinforces the general presumption that the Tribunal will have been given the powers necessary to fulfil its functions. We would say that Article 8, dealing with territorial jurisdiction, must be given some meaning. One might have thought that it was not necessary, because the crimes in question are defined elsewhere, but territorial jurisdiction has been hitherto an attribute of national courts exercising sovereign powers. One can say that the conferral of territorial jurisdiction implies that this Tribunal's powers will not be less than those that national courts might have, national courts which, of course, start out from the assumption of territorial jurisdiction. It is, of course, not the case that the Tribunal ceases to be an international tribunal by reason of its having those powers, but the combination of territorial jurisdiction and primacy must be given some effect. On the other hand, there is an important limitation, which is clearly intended in the Statute, and that is that the substantive trial jurisdiction of the Tribunal is limited to natural persons. In international law, states are recorded as persons but the Statute uses the phrase "person" in an entirely consistent way. Throughout, the term "person" means natural person. It does not mean corporation; it does not mean organisation. It does not mean government and it does not mean state. Under the Statute, and in this it is absolutely clear and in conformity with international law in relation to war crimes and crimes against humanity, the fact that the person on trial held or holds an official position is completely irrelevant. That person is accountable for his or her acts irrespective of official position, irrespective of Article 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: First, could you slow down, please? The interpreters have asked me twice and I know I speak very quickly also, but would you slow down? Your reference, though, to Article 6 and Article 7.1 have to do with jurisdiction over persons who may have committed crimes that are the subject matter jurisdiction of the Tribunal, so that really has nothing to do with whether or not we have authority to issue subpoenas to individuals who are neither suspects nor indictees. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Your Honour, as the Appeals Chamber pointed out in the Tadic case, it may be necessary, when one is dealing with procedural, or ancillary matters by analogy, to look at the structure of the document as a whole. I am making the point that the Tribunal -- the Statute of the Tribunal draws its own distinction between the state and persons. Persons include officials, but the state as a legal entity is not a body on trial. It is not an entity to be subjected to criminal sanctions as such under the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But the reference there in Article 7.1 is merely to state that there is no protection immunity from prosecution because of the fact that you hold that position, basically restating or reinforcing the Nuremburg Charter principle. That is all that -- PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Indeed, but it is important in the context of the Statute as a whole. The Statute in association with the Rules envisages in a number of contexts that where action is taken, or where a state fails to comply with its obligations, that the measures that will be taken take the form of reporting that failure to the Security Council. There are four rules, rules 11, 13, 59(B) and 61(E) which envisage that. It was a fair inference, looking at the Statute and the rules together, that the Statute does not envisage criminal sanctions directed at the state as such as a separate person. On the other hand, it is an equally fair inference that it may envisage criminal sanctions directed at persons who may be state officials or have been state officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Statute certainly does not envisage that states will be tried for criminal offences. Again from the Nuremburg Charter we are applying individual criminal responsibility. Thus there is a need to make it very clear in Article 7.1 that that is the situation, and I understand you take the position that penalties cannot be imposed against the state. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: As such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As such, but the authority to issue subpoenas and the authority, if authority exists, to exact penalties has nothing to do, I suppose, with the subject matter jurisdiction, except for one amicus that suggests there is a problem because of Rule 77 not speaking to contempt, except in two situations. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, Rule 77, of course, uses the word "persons" in exactly the same way as the rest of the Statute and Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: All I am saying is that the division that you make between state responsibility and individual responsibility I am not certain is transferable to the notion that states cannot be penalised for their non-compliance with orders issued by the Tribunal simply because they are not mentioned in Article 7 or Article 6, because those Articles deal with whether or not persons may be the subject of criminal prosecutions. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: The question is whether a power can be inferred -- and I said that the principle of effectiveness may have its limits -- the question is whether the power can be inferred without having been expressed from the Statute that this Tribunal can impose sanctions on the state as such in respect of its failures. What we say is that there is nothing in the Statute and Rules which would lead one to draw that inference, and there are various things in it which would lead one to draw the contrary. That is as far as I would put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What leads us to draw the contrary is that we may not try states for commission of war crimes and crimes on humanity. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: That is one indication, and also the four indications in the Rules that where states fail to comply with obligations, that this will be reported to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That argument does not help you. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, if the Tribunal had an inherent power itself to inflict penalties on those states, one might well have adopted your view that why should the Tribunal go running off to the Security Council? Why does the rule provide for access to the Security Council if the Tribunal can fix the matter itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Because in every Rule where there is a provision for non-compliance, all of the Rules speak to the Tribunal reporting to the Security Council. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Those particular Rules do, but, of course, Rule 77 refers to persons. Of course, the validity of Rule 77 is not directly in issue in these proceedings, because no invocation of that has yet been made. What is in issue in these proceedings is the sovereign immunity of Croatia from a subpoena, which we take to be an order, an order of a compelling sort, but an order that it provide certain documents. Our position is that the Tribunal has the power to issue such an order. There is no sovereign immunity in respect of that order, and, further, that the Tribunal has the power to determine compliance with that order, but that in the event the order is made directly against the state as such, the Tribunal has no further inherent power to impose sanctions. The existence of Rule 77 itself speaks against that, because it is an express power in respect of persons, and, as Professor Condorelli said, one would not infer a sanction power out of nothing. The mere use of the term "subpoena" in a rule is certainly not enough to incorporate common law rules about the inherent power of common law courts, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If we did not have Rule 77, would you take that same position? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, the question is how far the inherent power of the Tribunal in respect of persons extends, and that is a difficult question. If the Tribunal accepts our view that a subpoena is in effect even in respect of a subpoena, is an order to a person in effect to appear as a witness and speak to the existence and authenticity of documents, then the matter is covered under Rule 77 and the issue of inherent power does not arise, but I will leave my senior, the Prosecutor, to deal with that issue when she comes back to the question of enforcement. I am dealing with the basic question, which is whether the Tribunal has the power to issue an order to the state to provide documents, and our submission is that it clearly does under the Statute and that the rules in that respect merely reflect power already given by the Statute. Your Honour, I was drawing a distinction between the position of this Tribunal with respect to the former Yugoslavia and its position with respect to what I would describe as third states, states outside the former Yugoslavia. Of course, the relevant rules with respect to the gathering of evidence draw no distinction based upon the location of the state or the whereabouts of the state. They apply equally to all states, but there is an important difference in the incidence of those rules. The Tribunal is required by the Security Council Resolution establishing it and by its Statute to enquire into crimes committed in the context very largely of state acts in the former Yugoslavia. It is required to go into the question who committed those acts. Under what authority is irrelevant. Who committed them? At what level is irrelevant. In that context one can well imagine that a court required to conduct an effective trial will have to enquire into the acts of individual officials in considerable detail. So that the occasion for the exercise of investigative powers given to the Tribunal is likely to be considerably greater, massively greater, in respect of entities within the former Yugoslavia than it is with respect to third states. As a practical matter, the Tribunal will rely heavily upon the cooperation of states inside and outside the former Yugoslavia, but, of course, it will be very specially reliant upon the cooperation of third states, who have no direct interest, and there will be no assumption that third states are doing anything else but seeking to cooperate with the Tribunal. What the position is with respect to the former Yugoslavia is an empirical matter and it will be a matter for the Tribunal itself to judge as the occasion requires, whether the mechanism of cooperation or the mechanism of, one might say, coercion; that is to say the mechanism of imposing a requirement is the appropriate mechanism. In the question of third states it would overwhelmingly be the case that the method of cooperation will suffice. Of course, those third states are under an obligation to cooperate, but normally it will be sufficient to seek their cooperation and to rely upon their compliance with their international obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think you are perhaps more optimistic than circumstances have revealed themselves, because I am not certain how many states have enacted implementing legislation. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: I think it is 19 at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I did not know it was as many as 19. I thought it was maybe 12. Certainly that does show that the world community is coming to recognise their responsibility. In your brief you have stated there is coercive authority over the states in former Yugoslavia, rather, that obligation is coercive and in other states it is mandatory. That is a legal word of art under international law, and again what is the basis for that position, because Croatia takes the position that that would violate principles of international law, to provide two different obligations for states under Chapter 7. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: The obligations for states to comply with requests and orders under Article 29 is the same for all states of the world. That is what Article 29 says. What I am saying is the Prosecutor in seeking assistance and the court in issuing orders would, one assumes, take into account -- it will be a matter of judgment in each case -- whether it is appropriate to use the assistance mode or the mode of issuing orders. Professor Condorelli referred to that distinction as being merely statistical, although he acknowledged it existed. In three years of its operation, I am instructed, it has not been necessary for the Prosecutor to issue orders to third states on any occasion. It has all been done by the mechanism of request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That may be the reason the other states have not passed any legislation. That may be the reason. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It may be and that will be a question for the developing experience of the Tribunal. Obviously there is some interplay here between the effectiveness of the Tribunal in particular cases in obtaining long-term cooperation. Those are questions of judgment. It is not suggested that the power is intrinsically any different but the occasions for its exercise may well be different in the light of the purposes of the Tribunal and the fact that this is a Chapter 7 measure directed at the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What did you mean by "coercive" versus "mandatory"? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: That was a quotation from the Appellate Chamber's decision in the Tadic case. It is a question what the distinction between "coercive" and "mandatory" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We looked at that. I do not have the Tadic decision with me. I thought you had really quoted it out of context. I think we are going to stand in recess. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. When we return, we will have looked at the Tadic decision, and we can talk about it. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Thank you, your Honour. (4.05 pm) (Short break) (4.25 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Crawford, "coercive" versus "mandatory", you are correct; the Appeals Chamber does use it. I think it is on page 15. I have lost my note. Is it on page 15? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It is paragraph 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What page is that? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It is page 15 of this document, paragraph 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I was thinking when I first read it what they meant was that it was coercive in that the establishment of the Tribunal itself was for the purpose of bringing about an end to violations of -- serious violations of international humanitarian law but that the obligation was mandatory on others. The only reason I mention it is that Croatia has some concern about it but maybe we can hear from Croatia about it in that regard. It is not important. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Yes, your Honour, in which case I will move on. In some of the discussion the tendency has been to treat Article 29 of the Statute as concerned only with cooperation, but it is clear that Article 29 envisages both the obligation of states to comply with requests for assistance such as would be appropriate in the context of judicial cooperation, and also their obligation to comply with orders.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: The proposition that states are obliged to comply with orders carries with it the proposition that the order can be made to the state. It does not matter whether the source of the power to issue orders derives from Articles 19 and 20 or from Article 29 itself. They have to be read together. So it is clear from Article 29 that the Tribunal has the power to issue orders, as well as to make requests, in relation to the production of evidence. Those orders are binding, it is agreed by all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It uses two expressions, "request" and "order". PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Yes. A request, we submit, would be a request made in the normal course of events for judicial cooperation. That would be a request to a state or a state entity, or indeed it could be to someone else, but Article 29, paragraph 2, is addressing the obligation of the state to comply with such requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does it say -- this paragraph mentions two words, request for assistance or order, this very paragraph. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Yes. What we say is that it follows clearly that the Trial Chamber has the competence to issue orders to states in respect of the production of evidence. It is only if it had that competence that the question of compliance with the order could arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It does not limit the nature of the order. The words "including but not limited to". PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is a general sort of a power. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: A general power. Of course the request or order has to relate to the functions of the Tribunal and the Tribunal has its jurisprudence about the circumstances in which orders will be issued, but having been issued, states are obliged to comply with them. There is a distinction between the binding force of the order by virtue of Article 29 and the relevant Security Council Resolutions which expressly refer to Article 29 and the question how the order is to be enforced. The question of enforcement can only arise if the order is binding. It arises at a subsequent time. Croatia argues it is immune from the issue of the order by virtue of its status as a state, and that is contradicted by Article 29. The Security Council resolutions which, if necessary, make it clear, are, of course, Resolution 827 itself and then Resolution 1037, paragraph 20. I turn to the question of the term "subpoena" as it appears in Rule 54. The term "subpoena" has already been defined by the Prosecutor, and I will not add to what has been said. Obviously what that means is not to be derived necessarily from any individual legal system. It is a question what the Statute and the Rules provide that it means. It is certainly not in some sense ultra vires the Tribunal to use the word "subpoena" meaning a binding order in respect of the production of documents. It is a perfectly appropriate word to use. The fact that in a certain sense it reminds one of a particular legal system may or may not be unfortunate. How unfortunate it is tends to depend on how familiar one is with that legal system, but it is not ultra vires the Tribunal in its rule-making function under Article 15 to use the word "subpoena", by "subpoena" meaning an order in the nature of a requirement directed to a person to produce documents. That being so, the question is who may be the addressee of one of these orders called subpoenas? There is no limitation at all in Rule 54, nor is there any limitation on the addressees of orders in Articles 19 and 20 of the Statute. Article 29, of course, is concerned with the obligation of states, and if individuals do not comply with orders, it will be through the mechanism of states ultimately that those orders will be enforced, but if states themselves are bound by orders, there is no reason to think that anyone other than states will be bound by them either -- will not be bound by them either. So persons can be subject to orders and so can states. The question is: in those circumstances what is the position of state officials? I stress that we are talking about the binding character of the order. Now, it would be extraordinary if the Tribunal could issue orders to states but could not issue them to state officials. After all, those orders will at some point have to be complied with by persons acting ex officio. There may be circumstances in which it is appropriate or even necessary for the Tribunal to identify the person who will comply with its order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In this context I refer you to Article 18, Subsection 2, where the Prosecutor can seek the assistance of state authorities, not the state. "Authorities" obviously means persons. So the Statute specifically empowers the Prosecutor at least to obtain the assistance of persons other than the state, state authorities, not the state. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Yes, sir. Professor Condorelli drew the inference, which we submit is correct, if the Prosecutor can do it by virtue of the power to seek assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: From authorities. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Yes, from authorities, that the Tribunal itself would have the same power by way of issuing orders which are necessary for the conduct of the trial, for example, under Article 20, paragraph 1. There is no limitation on the persons to whom those orders may be made. If they are necessary for the conduct of the trial, they may be made to state officials. Again, we would submit the distinction that I have mentioned between the states within the former Yugoslavia and third states does arise. It may well be appropriate in the case of third states in the mode of judicial cooperation either to use a designated authority of that state or simply to address the request to the state as such and leave the state to determine how to comply. That may also be appropriate in the context of states within the former Yugoslavia, but the Tribunal has a choice. If it is necessary for the due conduct of the trial to go further than that and to go to particular authorities or particular named individuals and to seek -- and to order them to provide documents, there is nothing in the Statute which deprives the Tribunal of that power. It is certainly necessary for the due exercise of its functions, and there is nothing which precludes the Tribunal from exercising that power at the level of the making of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The source once again of the power of the Tribunal to issue subpoenas to individuals is what, you tell me? I know you have said Article 6 and Article 7.1 but you might look at 18.2. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: No. I was using Articles 6 and 7 in the context of a broader enquiry as to the scope of the Tribunal's coercive powers with respect to states as against individuals. I am now addressing the separate question: what is the scope of the Tribunal's ancillary power to issue orders with respect to evidence? That power, in our submission, looking at the power of the Tribunal, is actually contained in Articles 19.2 and Article 20, paragraph 1 of the Statute and is confirmed and elaborated -- well confirmed it cannot be -- is elaborated in Rule 54. Article 29 is really concerned with the correlative question of the obligation of states once those Articles have been issued. Article 29, both paragraphs start with the words "States shall ..." do something. It is therefore addressed to the question what states should do when they are confronted with these orders, but, of course, it is relevant to the interpretation of the general powers that the Tribunal has under Article 19.2 from the time of the confirmation of the indictment, and Article 20, paragraph 1 in respect of a Trial Chamber to issue orders which are necessary for the conduct of a trial. There is no limitation on the addressees of those orders. They could be persons or they could be state officials or they could be states. I suppose that if the only provisions of the Statute were Articles 19 and 20, you might say, applying reasoning such as Professor Malanczuk has advocated, that there is no express authority to issue orders to states, but that issue is completely precluded once you read Article 29. It is perfectly clear from Article 29 that orders can be issued to states. The source of the power to do so we say derives from Articles 19 and 20, on condition that the orders are necessary for the conduct of the trial, and the source of the obligation of states to comply with the orders is Article 29. That being so, there is no reason to infer any limitation with respect to the addressees of orders so far as state officials are concerned. Since orders can be directed to the state, they can equally be directed to officials of the state, and they can equally be directed to persons who are not officials at all. It is simply a question whether the particular order is necessary. As I was saying, in normal circumstances the Tribunal in the case of third states will not go behind the state, will simply address the state or a designated person for the purposes of cooperation and leave it at that, but if it is actually necessary in order to conduct a fair trial to go further, the Tribunal is empowered to do so. It has to exercise that discretion, and it will no doubt do so carefully, having regard to the sensitivities that undoubtedly exist, and which some of my professorial brethren have manifested in some of their submissions, but the power exists, because the overriding purpose of the Tribunal is to conduct a fair trial in respect of these serious crimes. Can I just say briefly in the context of state officials that the distinction that Professor Pellet sought to draw between officials acting in their public capacity and in their private capacity is not merely untenable but would cause a high degree of schizophrenia amongst the officials concerned. It seemed, as far as I could understand it, that the officials could be subpoenaed, as it were, in their personal capacity but not in their public capacity! I am not sure whether Professor Pellet was saying what they learned in their bathrooms they could disclose but not what they learned in their studies, and that in their professional capacity they were not allowed to disclose to themselves what they knew in their personal capacity. In real life we know things. We do not know them in capacities. However much distinction that validity might have in other contexts, since the Tribunal can issue orders to states, it can also issue orders to state officials. There is no third category of state officials as compared to states and persons and the Tribunal, having power over state and persons, has power over state officials as well. The exercise of those powers is a different matter and the Tribunal no doubt will exercise due caution. It has to be necessary, but that is a separate issue. Can I turn briefly to two remaining questions? The first is the question of so-called sovereign immunity. The second is the question of the status of national cooperation laws such as the law that Croatia has enacted and relies on as the exclusive channel of communication so far as the Tribunal is concerned. Dealing with the issue of sovereign immunity, we submit that sovereign immunity has nothing to do with this case. Sovereign immunity in international law is a doctrine applicable to national courts, to the courts of a particular state hearing cases involving foreign states. This is an international court and the doctrine of state immunity has no application. In international courts states are protected by the ordinary documents of consent to jurisdiction and so on, but this Tribunal having been validly established under the United Nations' Charter, to which all relevant states are parties, the issue of consent does not arise. There is no separate doctrine of immunity with respect to the proceedings of an international tribunal having jurisdiction in a given case and having the authority to issue orders to states generally. There is no, as it were, ghost in the machine which can then emerge and provide a degree of unspecified and unwarranted protection. Of course, the interests of states confronted with request is another matter, and the Prosecutor will return to that question in the context of the protection of confidentiality. No doubt the interests represented by the doctrine of sovereignty may be relevant at some stage in assessing whether it is really necessary to issue an order, or whether it is appropriate to use the cooperation, the means of cooperation rather than the means of issuing an order, but those are questions within the discretion of the Tribunal. They do not limit its power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any penalty we could impose on a state if there is no sovereign immunity vis a vis this Tribunal because it is an enforcement measure? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, the problem with respect to the state itself, and the Prosecutor will return to this issue -- the problem with respect to the state itself as distinct from its officials is that first of all there is no equivalent of Rule 77 which applies to the state. I mentioned earlier that the Statute and rules use the language of "person" in a completely consistent way and it is quite clear that Rule 77 has no application to the state as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And Rule 77 has no application to holding persons in contempt for failure to comply with subpoenas. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, that is a question which my leader will take up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Because in our view a subpoena is an order to someone to appear as a witness in order to testify as to the existence or genuineness of documents, but in any event I will leave that to my leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So there is no Rule 77. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: There is no Rule 77 and for the reasons I have already given there is no inherent power in the Tribunal, and certainly not by reason of the mere use of the word "subpoena" to inflict unspecified penalties on states as such, but I would incorporate what the Tribunal's friend and my friend, Professor Condorelli, said in respect of the idea of penalty. It may well be that the report of a particular state as non-complying, and of course the Tribunal has certainly inherent authority to determine compliance -- we would go further and say that the Tribunal's determination of non-compliance is binding, so that the Tribunal determines in the same way that the decisions of the UN Administrative Tribunal were binding on the Security Council. So the Tribunal determines there has been non-compliance and reports that to the Security Council. It is then -- this may be regrettable -- but it seems to us to follow from the present structure of the Statute and Rules -- it is then a matter for the Security Council to decide what to do, but the mere judicial determination with authoritative binding effect of this Tribunal that there has been a breach of a subpoena is itself a significant event. Now, it may well be that the Tribunal could give consideration to a Rule 77 bis. That might raise issues of validity, but they do not arise in this case. The issue in this case is whether the order can be issued to Croatia and whether Croatia has immunity has immunity and the answer is clearly "no".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Where is the inherent power inherent in the Statute to issue a penalty to an individual. I understand we have Rule 77 and perhaps there is an authority in terms of persons who appear before the Tribunal, an inherent authority that any court has, but for individuals who fail no comply with subpoenas, where is the inherent authority in the Statute? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Article 15 gives the Tribunal the power to make rules in respect of evidence and procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But the rules cannot go beyond obviously the constituent -- PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: The question of the validity of Rule 77 would raise the question whether Rule 15 authorised the enactment of Rule 77 in light of the Statute as a whole and its requirement that the Tribunal conduct effective trials. Effective criminal trials require some coercive power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: To whomever is the subject of a subpoena? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Yes. Well, with the exception that in other respects the structure of the Statute and Rules does draw a distinction between states and persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Again, where is the inherent power in the Statute to assess penalties against individuals? I understand Rule 15 and we have enacted 77 but maybe we are wrong. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, that is a matter for another case in the event you do enact penalties and they are challenged. We were certainly not in any sense seeking to question the validity of Rule 77, but Rule 77 is an expressly enacted rule. There is no equivalent rule enacted with respect to states, and at the very least if the Tribunal wishes to establish a mechanism which does not exist in the international system of the imposition of penalties on states, one would expect to find provisions -- procedural provisions and so on dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So there is no expression in the statute of any inherent authority to assess penalties against individuals but we have done that in Rule 77. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Well, in any situation you have to ask whether the particular rule is necessary for the effective furtherance of the purposes of the Tribunal having regard to the principle of interpretation which I have outlined. If necessary, we would submit that Rule 77 is a valid exercise of the rule-making power, because, in order to conduct an effective criminal trial, the Tribunal needs a certain level of coercive authority with respect to witnesses and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. So there is no specific mention in the Statute of inherent authority, but it is the inherent authority that all courts have with respect to individuals. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: We would say that is correct, but we would say that presumption which arises from the principle of effectiveness as I have articulated it is qualified with respect to states, both by the limits on the jurisdiction of the Tribunal expressed in the Statute and also the approach which the Tribunal itself took in the context of the rules to what it should do in the case of state non-compliance on four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is true except that in limits of our jurisdiction that refers to subject matter jurisdiction, and the rules that you referred to, 11, 59 and 61, deal with pre-initial appearance. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: Yes, they do. That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Tribunal at that point has not began their machinery of exercising their judicial functions. I think I understand you. We have at least taken a position in Rule 77 that we have that power and have not done so. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: In relation to individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: With respect to individuals and have not done so. One amicus states that there was no criticism of Rule 77. I cannot believe that but I accept what he says, maybe because there has been so much criticism of everything. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It remains to be seen whether there will be criticism of it. We do not say that it is not necessary and on the contrary there is a very good argument it is necessary. It is not at question in this case. The question is whether the Tribunal can issue an order to a state or state official and the answer is plainly "yes".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Rule 77 is very specific about the persons who can be committed for contempt. It would not in terms apply to a person not complying with the subpoena in this. It talks about a person who contumaciously refuses to answer a question or interrogates a witness. It is much more specific. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It may be that procedurally -- I do not want to trespass on what my learned senior will say -- it may be that procedurally where there is non-compliance with the subpoena there need to be further steps before Rule 77 comes into operation. That is a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have to rely on our inherent power as a court. PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: It is always a question of judgment how far the inherent power goes. We have simply submitted there are contraindications, that it goes so far as to impose penalties on the state as such as there are very considerable procedural difficulties on imposing sanctions on the state qua state, in terms of who is the entity to appear and so on. You only have to look at the experience of national jurisdictions dealing with states who are usually as such immune from any form of sanction even in respect of non-compliance with binding orders. Even in the context of corporate criminal liability, a fortiori the state, we would simply say the that as a matter of judgment the presumption of effectiveness in respect of the Tribunal the Statute does not go that far. Can I deal just finally with the issue of the law on cooperation? Clearly where a state enacts a law on cooperation, whether the state is within the former Yugoslavia or not, that provides a modality for cooperation with the state, and it would, assuming that the circumstances indicate that cooperation will be forthcoming -- it would usually be the mechanism which was used but a state cannot limit its international obligations by its national law; that is perfectly clear. Therefore, a state cannot provide that the only mechanism that shall be used is a law on cooperation. Article 29 imposes an international obligation on the state with which it must comply in terms determined by the Tribunal and not another statement. That completes my submissions, if it please the court, although I would be happy to answer any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Crawford. The Prosecutor? Presentation by Justice Arbour JUSTICE ARBOUR: Thank you very much, your Honour. I have essentially two remaining points to address and I will be very brief. The first one is the question of how does the current statutory framework, that is the Statute and the Rules, offer adequate protection to legitimate state interest in protecting matters of national security, executive privilege or any other form of validly recognised grounds for confidentiality? In my submission once again we find in this rather terse Statute of 34 Articles and in these Rules that are also not very extensive a perfectly adequate framework to answer that question within the context of a criminal system that fully recognises the compellability of all states and individuals for the production of evidence. Starting, first, with the Statute, Article 20 that I have referred to before imposes a duty on the Trial Chamber to conduct a fair and expeditious trial according to the rules, and Article 15 then grants the power to make the rules. Now if I may turn to Rule -- I have them here -- to Rules 89 and 95, and I will start, if I may, with Rule 95. That Rule is a very broad and generous exclusionary Rule, which provides that: "No evidence shall be admissible if attained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." Rule 89 is also a rule of exclusion of evidence and in particular subsection (d) provides that: "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." In my submission, fairness of the trial is a concept broad enough in any jurisdiction which rests on the rule of law to encompass fairness to all participants, not only to the Prosecution and to the accused, but to witnesses. These rules of exclusions are broad enough even in a context which has other specific exclusionary rules to provide a discretion in the court, for instance, to balance the probative value of a piece of evidence that is tendered by a party against, for instance, important concerns of privacy of the witness, and in exercising its discretion a Trial Chamber would very readily, in my submission, under these two rules, come to the conclusion that they are interests that can be adequately protected in the context of a fair trial by excluding relevant evidence, weighing that against its probative value, its materiality, in a context, of course, where this evidence is properly compelled. Compellability of evidence, I think, ought not to be confused with its ultimate admissibility. Within that framework it is my submission that any valid national security interest can very readily be accommodated by this Tribunal under these broad exclusionary powers. This is very early in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, so we do not have a lot of guidance from decisions, but as has been mentioned before, these questions of privilege or exception, claims of national security or state secret, are extraordinarily fact-sensitive. It requires a balancing, which, on the one hand, necessitates an appreciation of the relevance and the probative value of the evidence that is sought to be tendered and, on the other hand, of the cogency and the potency of the claim that it ought to be excluded to protect a legitimate state interest. Now this, of course, comes after that there has been a full scrutiny of whether the evidence that is being sought is relevant, is material, is sufficiently targeted and clearly identified. All these objections, of course, can be made by the recipient of the subpoena, who, compelled as he may be, is entitled to challenge the breadth of the subpaenas, the scope of it, the relevancy of the evidence that is being sought, and it is in that form, in my submission, that the recipient of the subpoena has ample room to assert before this Tribunal an interest that the Tribunal can very well balance against the interests of the party seeking to produce that evidence. So, in my submission, we do not even have to go to a more elaborate statutory scheme, even though one of the briefs of the amicus suggests that it might be desirable for the Tribunal to enact a much more specific regulatory scheme to protect these kinds of interests. The sole privilege or exception, if we may want to call it this way, which is specifically provided for in the Rule is the solicitor-client privilege, but in my submission this does not preclude the court from exercising it's discretion under the rules that it ought to conduct a fair hearing to protect other interests that belong to witnesses who have to be called upon to be participants in this form. So, in my submission, it is premature in this form to start addressing the details of what this national security exception -- how it should operate and what it would look like. It would certainly be my submission that the Tribunal could easily develop different levels of scrutiny. For instance, when the privilege or the exception is asserted by a state which has otherwise been a cooperative state with no interest either way on the outcome of the case, the court may develop a level of scrutiny that is more deferential to the claim of privilege than it would be, for instance, in a state that has certainly an apparent interest in the outcome of the case, or certainly on the issue that is being addressed by the evidence that is sought by the parties, and that has a history of non-cooperation, in which case the level of scrutiny of the assertion of privilege might be somewhat higher. This is way down the road, it seems to me, in terms of developing a jurisprudence that will be illustrative of this balancing exercise that is perfectly open to the Tribunal. So my submission is this is where this very legitimate concern is addressed and not by a unilateral denial of compellability, which, as we have illustrated before, is simply not open under a proper interpretation of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. There are a number of things that you have said. One, should we apply a different standard to a state simply because it has "not cooperated in the past"? It seems to me that perhaps we should take each issue as it comes and not assume that because a state, for whatever reason, has not cooperated in the past, and then subject that state to a different scrutiny, suggesting that they are not really truthful -- that is about what it amounts to -- in their assertion, or that we are further going to penalise them, now that we have them, in such a way to get back at them for not cooperating. We do not want to do that, do we? I perhaps misunderstood what you said. JUSTICE ARBOUR: I do not want to suggest a standard that is any way vindictive or punitive. My submission is essentially this is a quintessential case that is extremely fact-sensitive, and that absent a claim in this particular instance of such an interest, we have no factual underpinning upon which to engage usefully in this kind of exercise. There are several factors and I think a history of bona fide compliance could be -- certainly is one that the Prosecutor would want to advance, if appropriate, on the facts of a given case as relevant to the level of scrutiny that the privilege or the exception should be admitted to; for instance, as to whether the court should be prepared to simply defer to the claim of privilege by its very nature or else, and in my submission it would almost invariably be more appropriate, embark on some kind of examination of the foundation of the privilege in camera or whatever format is then appropriate. This is all, in my submission, down the road, but I just wanted to make clear that there is ample room within the framework of our proceedings to ensure that these legitimate and valid interests can be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do not know about that then, because when you referred to our evidence re rules, what you are saying is that on 89(D): "The Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." That begs -- it does not beg the issue -- it does not even address the issue of whether or not the evidence should even be produced by a state to the Prosecutor for its use, and then, when it is attempted to be used, the court makes a determination that the probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The issue is whether or not a state is obligated to disclose to (a) the Prosecutor or perhaps even the Trial Chamber material which it considers to be protected for national security reasons. So the fact that it may not be admitted in trial does not really resolve that issue, because the damage has already been caused, on the part of the state at least, because the Prosecutor has it. JUSTICE ARBOUR: I would submit, coming back to the original analysis that I put forward, that when we are in the post-indictment phase of the proceedings, for all practical purposes the subpoena or any other means of compelling evidence is a mechanism that is ultimately geared to the conduct of the trial. If, for instance, there could be a serious claim that the evidence that we are seeking to get access to in this case was so immaterial that it could not possibly be admissible at trial, in my submission it would be a proper ground for this Chamber to deny access, which is a completely different issue than the issue on which we were here today, whether we have the legal power to compel access to the evidence. Now whether this evidence is protected by -- some of it may be protected by a solicitor-client privilege, and it ought to be asserted, if that is the case, but in my submission, if the evidence was not to be properly admissible at trial, then I would concede that it ought not to be properly disclosed or discoverable by the Prosecutor in a trial preparation phase through the use of a court order. I will make that concession. So the ultimate test is the test of admissibility at trial. That is what determines whether the subpoena should be executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It may be admissibility at trial, because it may be relevant, but it still may be privileged on the part of the state and thus not subject to a subpoena that would allow the Prosecutor or the defence, even, to look at evidence. So it may very well be admissible, it may be relevant, but it is still protected because there are some very serious national security questions involved. So that is another way to protect it, but we still have not resolved the first issue, and that is whether or not the state is required to give to the Trial Chamber material that is the subject of a subpoena if it claims that it is protected by national security or military secret privilege. Should they give that to the Trial Chamber for review to determine whether or not that claim is legitimate, or do they have a blanket right to make that claim, or must they make the claim and then substantiate it with something? That is the issue. Those are the issues. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Yes. In my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How do we resolve those? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Well, maybe I misspoke myself when I spoke of admissibility. If evidence is relevant but it is barred by a privilege, in my submission it is not admissible and it is in that sense --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But you do not get it to begin with. JUSTICE ARBOUR: That is right. I concede that. If you cannot show that the evidence sought is both relevant, material and not barred by any rule of exclusion, then you cannot get it. You can only get the evidence if you can demonstrate that it is relevant, material and otherwise admissible at trial. So the party wanting to resist the subpoena is entitled to say: "The evidence you are seeking from me is barred, for instance, by the solicitor-client privilege." That determination has to be made prior to any disclosure to the Prosecutor but presumably it cannot be made just by asserting it. You have to produce some indication to the court that, in fact, the document, say, that is being sought is a document that is covered by the umbrella of solicitor-client privilege. In my submission it is exactly the same thing with respect to an assertion of national security or privilege. It is a matter for determination the first time around, either in a pre-trial phase or at trial, for the court to determine whether the privilege is validly asserted. Now, what level of scrutiny would be the appropriate one? In the abstract I suppose one could imagine cases where the court would not even want to look at the content of the document, could be satisfied on all the other circumstances that the relevancy is so marginal, the probative value is so marginal, and that on its face there is such a plausible claim of state security that the court may even defer and make the decision without examining the content. In my submission, these would be rare occasions. More commonly, the court would engage in this balancing exercise probably wanting to examine in camera and keep sealed in the court documents, if it had to, the materials on which secrecy is being claimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In your brief you take the position that, in respect to national security interests or other sensitive information, that the Trial Chamber should be permitted to review such information or evidence and then make a finding that the purported interests of the state and non-disclosure outweighs the manifest interests of the International Criminal Tribunal and the Security Council in ensuring the effect of prosecutions of serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So is it your position that the Trial Chamber has a right to review the documents when there is a claim made that they are protected by national security interests? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Otherwise -- and just -- this will be my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Tell me what support you have for that in the citations that you have given us. For example, from the United States in the Reynolds case followed by Nixon, which you cite on page -- it is here somewhere -- I thought you cited it? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Yes, we did cite it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do not read Reynolds that way. JUSTICE ARBOUR: If I may just come back to the original point on whether or not a mere statement of the privilege would bar any further scrutiny, in my submission that is an untenable position if we are correct on the threshold issue of compellability. If the Tribunal has the power to compel from states and individuals testimonial and documentary evidence, obviously it cannot concede that by merely raising a claim of national security it would be yielding its authority to compel. So, in my submission, the mere raising of a claim of national security has to be on its face insufficient. Now, what more needs to be done for the court to be satisfied that on balance it should respect the claim of privilege? I can only say it will vary from case to case, but let me maybe say at the outset: there are very few jurisdictions which now would tolerate an absolute and unreviewable claim of state secret, executive privilege or national security privilege in a criminal prosecution. Now, I will concede once again that we are in a very different legal environment. In a domestic jurisdiction there is unity of interest in the state. It is a fair assumption, certainly supported by the law of most states, that the state has an equal interest in protecting criminals and in protecting the secrecy of its national security, and, if absolutely pressed, the state itself will make the decision and could possibly make the decision not to prosecute. So if at some point there was a genuine risk that in order to come to a fair and reliable disposition of a criminal case, where guilt or innocence turns on access to a piece of evidence that could be protected by national security, a state may be forced to choose between its dual competing public interest, state security or law enforcement. Now, we are in a context in which we do not have the luxury of deferring to the state making that adequate choice, because what is really competing here is not the national interest of a state in protecting, say, its military secrets and its interest in law enforcement; the balancing exercise, in my submission, that the Tribunal has to embark upon is the competing interest of the international community, on the one hand of ensuring that the crimes that are within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal are fully and adequately prosecuted -- that is one interest -- and, on the other hand, of respecting the genuine, well-founded sort of privacy interest of persons and security interest of states. I concede that there is an international community interest in not unduly violating domestic state secrets, but there is also an international community interest in ensuring that crimes within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal are prosecuted to the fullest and field a reliable conviction or acquittal. In that case we cannot turn to the state and say: "You make the choice" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Who do you mean by the state? A state judge or the prosecution? JUSTICE ARBOUR: The prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is exactly what I thought you meant. So in a domestic situation the prosecution make the decision: "We have this evidence and we have to make the decision whether we are going to go forward against this evidence. If we have to use evidence that may reveal national secrets, then we will not go forward." So that is all within the province of the Prosecutor's Office. JUSTICE ARBOUR: It could, although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So they make that decision. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Although under the mandate that has been given to the Prosecutor by the Security Council I do not think it is incumbent on the Prosecutor to uphold claims of national security interest. I believe that the Prosecutor is entitled to put his or her case to the Tribunal and it is in the Tribunal that these competing interests will be debated and the Tribunal will come to either the realisation that in this case the international community's interest will be better protected by either respecting the claim for privilege, particularly if the evidence sought is of minimal probative value, to take an extreme case -- if the court could come to the conclusion that it could easily respect, for instance, a claim of national security privilege without jeopardising the reliability of the fact-finding process, because if the evidence sought is either merely corroborative of other evidence or is of trivial probative value, that is the easy case. There are other instances where the evidence sought seems to be crucial to a just and reliable disposition of the case, and where the national security that is being asserted has no credible basis, either in fact or in law, in which case the court would reject the privilege. These cases, even domestically, are not frequent, so it is difficult to have the full spectrum of these kinds of dispositions. My submission is the court can have -- this Tribunal has full compellability power and a full capacity within the framework of the Statute to respond very adequately to these very legitimate concerns but they have to be addressed with the full factual underpinning to give an air of reality to a debate that is otherwise, I think, extremely speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do not know. It just seems to me then, if anything, the state before our Tribunal is in need of greater protection, because, if I understand your argument, and I am not sure I fully understand it, in a domestic situation it would be the Prosecutor that would probably make the determination: "Can we make this case without violating national security interests?" If they make the determination that that cannot happen, then they will not go forward. So in a sense the Prosecutor is assisting in almost protecting the state by making decisions about what cases it will prosecute, and if there is a need to violate national interest. Here, though, the Prosecutor does not have an interest in that at all. The Prosecutor has an interest in bringing a case. Only the Tribunal then has an interest in perhaps stopping the disclosure of national security interests, and, if so, it seems to me that we should be very careful in that exercise. JUSTICE ARBOUR: I certainly concede the need for prudence. One must, of course, realise that the materials that are sought by this kind of order could be sought by the defence as well. This question has been alluded to before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. JUSTICE ARBOUR: On that point all I can say once again is that these issues are extremely fact-sensitive. If the defence was seeking production of information from a state and the state was claiming that the evidence ought not to be produced because of a national security interest, once again in my submission the court would have to engage in this balancing test of trying to determine the potential probative value of the evidence against the severity of the injury that would be inflicted to the state's interest if the evidence was being produced. Now what would be the ultimate result, I hate to even imagine a case scenario as what has been even alluded to before, but in my submission if the court was to come to the conclusion that the evidence is critical to the entitlement of the defence to lay the foundation for an acquittal, and at the same time it could not compel, for instance, because the evidence was in the hand of a state against which means of enforcements are somewhat limited, and therefore it came to the conclusion that the defence could not get access to a piece of evidence that would appear to be critical to its entitlement to be defended, presumably it could order that the proceedings be stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Or dismissed. JUSTICE ARBOUR: It does not lie with the Prosecutor to look at the Doomsday scenario for its case but that is the ultimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In such a case we will be transferring our judicial power to the case. It can solely determine whether the case can go on or the man be acquitted. Is really then the judge not this court? JUSTICE ARBOUR: In that case I hope the state would be answerable to public opinion and to the Security Council, not only for its lack of compliance, but for defeating in a very dramatic way the purpose for which the Tribunal was set up. So ultimately I would hope that if ever a case of this kind, offset with this kind of dilemma, presented itself factually, and my submission is that it will be -- it is a highly hypothetical case, where this evidence could not be obtained by any other means and could be demonstrated to be so probative of innocence that we could not proceed without it -- but if that were the case, the state in question would be answerable to the world community and certainly, I would hope, to the Security Council for having taken such an unacceptable position in the face of its obligation to cooperate with international criminal justice, but that is the end of the road, in my submission, for this kind of argument. If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Where are you going now? JUSTICE ARBOUR: The last submission I have to make is on the power of enforcement, Rule 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How long will you need for that? JUSTICE ARBOUR: I am going to need only ten minutes, if I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us continue on. We would normally finish at 5.30. Let us continue on and see if we can complete that portion. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Much has been said already so I think we can complete these submissions rapidly, if I can get to it. I just want to come back to my original submission that a subpoena is, contrary to what its Latin name seems to have indicated to some, not an exercise in punishment. It is an exercise in compellability. If the subpoena fails, and I will start with a natural person -- if a subpoena is addressed to a person, requiring that person to attend court and/or produce documents to the court, and there is non-compliance, in my submission it is appropriate to then turn to the witness and call for an explanation for the non-performance, for instance by issuing an order that the witness attend to show cause, and, frankly, whether we call it, to show cause why he or she should not be held in contempt, or merely be given a second opportunity to give an explanation for his non-compliance, again I do not think it is a critical distinction. Failing that, and assuming, first of all, that we could be certain that service of the subpoena has been effected -- for instance, in a case like this one where the recipient of the subpoena has had exchanges with the Tribunal, so we can be under no misapprehension that the party that is targeted knows of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: This is for Bosnia-Herzegovina. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Yes, and for the personal recipients of the subpoena, one of whom is represented by counsel here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. JUSTICE ARBOUR: So we know they are aware of the existence of the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is not the Croatian subpoena, though, that you are referring to? JUSTICE ARBOUR: That is right, and I am not making any submissions on whether or not there is evidence to suggest that the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia is unaware of the existence of the subpoena that has been issued against him. It has been duly served through the proper channels of communication with the Republic of Croatia. There has been no suggestion that it was not properly then delivered. So in my submission we could certainly proceed in this case with the fair assumption that the witness is aware of that order. Now, if there is non-attendance, I will be making submissions that we then fall squarely within Rule 77, but even before getting there, if I may, Rule 77 is an illustration of the need to give genuine meaning to the express compellability and to give real meaning to the court order. If the court has the power to issue a legally binding order compelling a person to attend court, it has to mean something more than you serve the order on the person and you wait and see whether voluntary compliance will be forthcoming. In my submission, it is open to the court, to the Tribunal, either on its own motion or at the request of a party, if there is non-compliance with a subpoena, to issue a warrant for the arrest of the person, thereby compelling his attendance in court. I will base my submission on the wording of the Statute itself, which once again is not extremely explicit. I think it has been clear in the course of today's argument of this Statute that, one, it is not always very explicit and, in my submission, does not have to be if it is read in a manner which is consistent with the principles that it should be read to achieve its purpose. If we may turn to Article 19, Article 19, subsection 2, provides that: "The judge may, at the request of the Prosecutor, issue orders and warrants for the arrest, detention, surrender or transfer of persons." It does not say "of accused". We are now post-indictment. The indictment has now been confirmed. The accused is at that point a legal entity. The distinctions between persons and accused cannot be viewed as accidental in this Statute. It -- the distinction is drawn consistently. If you turn to Article 21, paragraph 1: "All persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal." Starting at paragraph 2: "The following subsections convey rights that are conferred not on persons but on the accused". The language is extremely specific of what its intent is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have referred to Article 19, subsection 2. It starts with: "Upon confirmation of an indictment..." Then it talks about warrants of arrest, detention. On the face of it this probably means this refers to persons who have been indicted, not to other persons, if you read subsection 2. It starts with: "Upon confirmation of an indictment ..." The person charged is mentioned. Then it talks of the issuing of warrants. Obviously it refers to persons who have been indicted and not to witnesses or other persons.
